shiftMode: Call for help early — assign roles: airway, meds, monitor, suction, backup airway, post-intubation sedation.
Preoxygenate aggressively; consider NC apneic oxygenation, flush-rate NRB, NIV, or BVM with PEEP depending on physiology.
Have suction in hand or immediately reachable before the first attempt.
Choose first-pass and backup plans before pushing meds — video/direct laryngoscopy, introducer, supraglottic, cricothyrotomy.
Name plan and action together, never the letter alone: A tracheal intubation, B supraglottic airway, C final facemask attempt plus the wake-up-or-proceed decision, D front-of-neck access.
Maximum 3+1 attempts (DAS 2025): three, plus one final attempt by a more experienced colleague only. Change something material each attempt.
The plus-one is a handover, not an extra turn for the same operator. No one more experienced available: ceiling is three.
Hypoxemia at any point: abandon the attempt, prioritize facemask oxygenation. Oxygenate between attempts; maintain anesthesia.
Physiology kills before anatomy: optimize hypotension, hypoxemia, severe acidosis, RV failure, and hyperkalemia when possible.
Confirm with continuous waveform capnography; auscultation alone is not enough.
Give post-intubation analgesia and sedation, and reassess the ventilator.
indications: Failure to oxygenate or ventilate
Inability to protect airway
Expected clinical deterioration requiring airway control
Severe agitation or injury requiring controlled oxygenation/ventilation
Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest airway management when appropriate
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in a true airway emergency
Anticipated impossible oral intubation should trigger alternate plan early
Severe physiologic instability may require resuscitation before induction when time allows
Suspected cervical spine injury: not a contraindication to intubation or to paralysis. See positioning.
Adult scope only. Pediatric tube sizing, blade choice, cuffed-versus-uncuffed decision, per-kilogram dosing, and far shorter safe apnea time are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Align oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes when using direct laryngoscopy; ear-to-sternal-notch positioning helps many adults.
Identify epiglottis, arytenoids, posterior cartilages, and cords. Do not advance through unidentified tissue.
In obesity or pregnancy, ramp aggressively rather than placing the patient flat.
equipment: Monitor: cardiac monitor, pulse ox, BP cycling, waveform capnography ready
Preoxygenation setup: NRB, nasal cannula, BVM with PEEP, NIV as needed
Suction connected and tested
Video laryngoscope and/or direct laryngoscope with working light
ET tubes: planned size plus one size smaller
Stylet and bougie
10 mL syringe for cuff inflation and a cuff manometer
ETCO2 detector / continuous waveform capnography
Tube holder or tape
Backup supraglottic airway
Cricothyrotomy kit available for high-risk airway
Induction and paralytic medications drawn up and labeled
Post-intubation analgesia/sedation ordered or ready
positioning: Place patient ear-to-sternal-notch when possible.
Ramped position for obesity, pregnancy, or poor neck mobility.
Head elevated when tolerated to prolong safe apnea time.
Suspected cervical spine injury: minimize movement rather than immobilize rigidly. Manual in-line stabilization, jaw thrust rather than head tilt and chin lift, and videolaryngoscopy where available.
Remove the front of the collar for laryngoscopy and have the assistant hold the head.
steps: Assess airway difficulty and physiologic risk.
Preoxygenate and optimize hemodynamics before induction when possible.
Verbalize primary and backup airway plan.
Prepare equipment, suction, capnography, tube securement, and post-intubation medications.
Administer induction and paralytic medications when ready.
Perform laryngoscopy with deliberate epiglottis and glottic identification.

Pass the tube under continuous direct or video visualization. With a hyperangulated videolaryngoscope blade use a stylet, bougie, or flexible bronchoscope. Do not advance a bougie blind at a Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 view: DAS 2025 advises against it because of trauma and misplacement risk - improve the view first.

Between attempts, change something informed by the last one: position, laryngoscope or blade, introducer, operator, external laryngeal manipulation, suction, removal of cricoid force, or optimized neuromuscular block.
After 3+1 unsuccessful attempts declare 'failed intubation', move to Plan B, summon assistance, and make the eFONA kit immediately accessible.
Inflate the cuff to the minimum that stops the leak and measure it: 20-30 cmH2O. Milliliters are not a pressure - a 10 mL syringe emptied into the cuff overshoots.
Confirm continuous waveform capnography and bilateral chest rise; check for right mainstem.

Secure the tube at a documented depth - about 21 cm at the incisors in women and 23 cm in men, or three times the tube size - then obtain a chest x-ray when appropriate and reassess ventilator and sedation.
ultrasound: Adjunct for tube confirmation in some settings; continuous waveform capnography remains the standard when available.
confirmation: Two-point check (DAS 2025): the tube seen passing through the vocal cords AND sustained exhaled carbon dioxide on waveform capnography. Sustained capnography excludes esophageal placement but cannot by itself exclude bronchial or pharyngeal position.
Bilateral chest rise and breath sounds
Absent gastric insufflation sounds
Appropriate oxygenation/ventilation response
Chest x-ray for depth and complications when clinically appropriate
troubleshooting: Desaturation: stop, oxygenate with BVM/PEEP, improve mask seal, use oral/nasal airway, recruit help.

Poor view: optimize position, suction, external laryngeal manipulation (BURP on the thyroid cartilage), change blade or laryngoscope, optimize neuromuscular block. Do not insert a bougie blind at a grade 3-4 view.
Cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate: supraglottic airway or surgical airway pathway immediately.
Sugammadex reliance: it does not rescue a cannot-intubate cannot-oxygenate patient now. 16 mg/kg reverses rocuronium in about three minutes - oxygenate and go to the front of the neck.
Post-intubation hypotension: check tube depth, breath stacking/auto-PEEP, tension pneumothorax, sedation effect, occult shock; start fluids/pressors as appropriate.
High peak pressures: consider bronchospasm, tube obstruction, mainstem, pneumothorax, or ventilator mismatch.
complications: Failed airway requiring supraglottic or surgical airway
aftercare: Start analgesia and sedation immediately unless deliberately held for neurological assessment; if held, say so out loud to the team. Rocuronium outlasts a single induction dose by roughly 35 minutes - risk of awareness under paralysis.
Set ventilator based on disease state; reassess plateau pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamics.
Obtain chest x-ray when appropriate to confirm depth and evaluate complications.
Reassess tube depth after transport or major position changes.
documentation: Indication for intubation: airway protection, respiratory failure, or anticipated clinical deterioration.
Consent when feasible; emergency justification when delay would risk patient harm.
Preoxygenation and monitoring: cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, capnography.
Medications, as documented in MAR.
Tube placement under visualization and secured depth.
Devices used: laryngoscope and blade type, tube size, introducer, and any adjunct.
Number of attempts, what was changed between them, and the view obtained.
Difficulty encountered and how it was resolved. Difficult airway: verbal handover to the ongoing team plus a chart record, not the procedure note alone.
Confirmation: continuous waveform capnography and clinical assessment.
Tolerance of procedure; complications documented separately.
seniorPearls: Your first attempt should be your best attempt. Do not burn an attempt while still setting up.
If the patient is crashing from physiology, a beautiful view of the cords will not save them by itself.
Have the post-intubation plan ready before induction.
references: Ahmad I, El-Boghdadly K, Iliff H, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.10.006

Society of Critical Care Medicine. Clinical Practice Guidelines for Rapid Sequence Intubation in the Critically Ill Adult Patient. 2023. https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/guidelines-rapid-sequence-intubation

Difficult Airway Society, Association of Anaesthetists, British Society of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons, Intensive Care Society, NACCS, Faculty of Prehospital Care, Royal College of Emergency Medicine. Airway management in patients with suspected or confirmed cervical spine injury. 2024. https://das.uk.com/guidelines/cervical-spine-injury/
Verify local airway policy, kit contents, and medication protocols before use.

medicationDosing.indication: Rapid sequence induction and intubation, adult. Doses are targets, not ceilings.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Give an induction agent with the paralytic - never a paralytic alone. Choose the agent by physiology, not habit; see agent of choice below. In shock the two move in opposite directions: halve the induction dose and give the full paralytic dose, because a slow circulation delays onset and an underdosed paralytic leaves you a straining patient.

medications.caution: For raised ICP, pain, or tachycardia. Will drop the blood pressure in a patient who is already compensating: omit it or halve it in shock.
No analgesia. Brief myoclonus. Cortisol suppression may carry a negative prognostic implication in sepsis. Halve the dose in shock.

May induce cardiac ischemia or arrhythmias, and increases salivation. Use in raised intracranial pressure remains controversial. Not hemodynamically neutral in a catecholamine-depleted patient - the direct myocardial depression is unmasked once the sympathetic reserve is gone, so halve the dose in shock.
Hypotension, bradycardia, negative inotropy, and 2-5 minutes to peak. A last resort for induction when nothing else is available, not an equal alternative to the agents above.
Potent vasodilation and significant hypotension. Contraindicated with egg or soybean allergy. Dose on lean body weight, and halve it in shock.

DAS 2025 specifies 1.2 mg/kg for RSI; the lower end of this range gives slower onset and may not give RSI-grade conditions. Dose on ideal body weight. Outlasts a single induction dose by about 35 minutes - sedation afterwards is not optional.
Hyperkalemia risk. Avoid in malignant hyperthermia, neuromuscular disease, rhabdomyolysis, and stroke or burns more than 72 h old. Dose on total body weight.

medicationDosing.sourceNote: Doses from tl;dr pharmacy, 'The Pharmacist's Do's and Don'ts of Rapid Sequence Intubation' (2023), accepted by the clinical owner and re-affirmed unchanged on 2026-07-30. That source cites no primary references. Intravenous lidocaine and defasciculating vecuronium were removed from pretreatment on 2026-07-30: neither is supported by current evidence. Paediatric atropine is omitted because this record is adult-scoped.
selectionGuidance: Status epilepticus: etomidate, propofol, or midazolam.
Hemodynamic instability or distributive shock: etomidate or ketamine.
Severe bronchospasm: etomidate, ketamine, or propofol.

shiftMode: Confirm indication, site, side, anticoagulation/coagulopathy status.
Full sterile barrier: cap, mask, gown, gloves, wide chlorhexidine prep, large drape.
Ultrasound before puncture: identify vein, artery, thrombus, depth, compressibility, and safest trajectory.
Never dilate until Ultrasound confirms the wire in two planes, or transduce, every time — no emergency exception.
Keep control of the wire at all times.
Confirm placement and screen for complications per site and institutional practice.
indications: Vasopressor or irritant medication administration
Poor peripheral access with need for reliable central access
Central venous pressure monitoring
Massive transfusion or high-flow resuscitation when appropriate catheter chosen
Temporary access while definitive access is arranged
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection or burn over intended insertion site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at intended site
Uncorrected coagulopathy (relative)
anatomy: IJ: vein is commonly lateral/anterior to carotid but anatomy varies.
Femoral: NAVEL lateral-to-medial reminder is imperfect.
Subclavian/axillary access has pneumothorax and noncompressible bleeding considerations.
Always distinguish compressible vein from pulsatile/noncompressible artery before puncture.
equipment: Central line kit with catheter, wire, needle, scalpel, dilator, and caps
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape, chlorhexidine scrub
Ultrasound machine
Sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Sterile pressure tubing or manometry setup to confirm venous placement before dilation
Flushes for all ports
Suture or securement device
Biopatch or antimicrobial dressing
Transparent sterile dressing
Sharps container and sterile towels
Chest x-ray or confirmation
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, avoid excessive rotation.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Place the ultrasound screen in your line of sight before sterile prep.
steps: Confirm indication and choose site based on urgency, anatomy, infection risk, bleeding risk, and clinical need.
Perform ultrasound survey before opening the kit.
Prep and drape using full sterile barrier technique.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along planned tract.
Cannulate vein under ultrasound guidance, maintaining needle tip awareness.
Pass the guidewire smoothly without force, keeping a hand on it at all times.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating: ultrasound in short and long axis planes. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce or manometer before dilating.
Make small skin nick while controlling wire.
Dilate over wire without force; stop if resistance or uncertainty.
Advance catheter over wire, remove wire while maintaining catheter control, and state aloud that the wire is out and intact while looking at it.
Occlude every hub the moment the wire is out - cap, clamp, or connected tubing - so the catheter is never open to air.
Aspirate and flush all ports.
Secure catheter and apply sterile dressing.
Confirm position.
ultrasound: Use short-axis for vessel identification; consider long-axis for needle tip tracking if skilled.
Compress vein before sterile prep to evaluate patency and thrombus.
Confirm the guidewire in the vein in two planes before dilation - short axis to exclude the artery, long axis to show it tracking centrally.
confirmation: All ports aspirate and flush easily
Guidewire removed intact and confirmed aloud
Catheter secured with sterile dressing
Appropriate imaging/confirmation obtained based on site
Tip at the SVC/right atrial junction on chest x-ray, at or just above the carina
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude arterial placement; transduce the catheter if there is any doubt
No immediate evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; check needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Color, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not answer it.

Arterial puncture with the needle only (18 G or smaller, not dilated): withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. After a neck puncture watch the airway for several hours - a carotid hematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it and do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and call vascular surgery and interventional radiology now. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, hemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Resistance with dilator: stop; confirm wire path and vessel location before proceeding.
No blood return from one port: check clamp/cap, flush gently, reposition; do not force against resistance.

Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub: suspect air embolism - occlude the hub, left lateral decubitus head-down, 100% oxygen, and aspirate from a central lumen if one is in place.
Unstable after line: consider pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or unrelated shock progression.
complications: Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian/axillary approaches
aftercare: Label line and date dressing per local policy.
Review imaging/confirmation before using for high-risk infusions if required by site/policy.
Remove unnecessary lines as soon as clinically appropriate.
Reassess insertion site for bleeding or hematoma after placement.
documentation: Indication for central venous catheter.
Consent, or emergent need if consent not possible.
Site and side; full sterile barrier precautions.
Ultrasound guidance for vessel identification and cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance, removed intact.
All ports aspirated and flushed; catheter secured with sterile dressing.
Placement confirmation and immediate complication assessment.
seniorPearls: The catastrophic errors come after venous puncture, not before: wire control, dilation, confirmation.
If the wire does not pass smoothly, the answer is never more force.
Open the exact catheter you need. A triple lumen is not a Cordis and not a dialysis catheter.
After two failed passes, change something: the site, the operator, or the plan.
If a large-bore device ends up in an artery, leave it in and make the call.

visualAssets.title: IJ ultrasound probe orientation
visualAssets.subtitle: Short-axis view of IJ vein and carotid artery. Probe marker toward patient's right. Vein is compressible, lateral and superficial to the artery.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Confirm vein vs. artery with compression before needle entry.

visualAssets.title: Sternocleidomastoid triangle
visualAssets.subtitle: The IJ vein runs between the two heads of the SCM. The apex of the triangle at the clavicle is the traditional landmark insertion point.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Always use ultrasound guidance. Landmark-only technique increases complication risk.

visualAssets.title: Wire position confirmation
visualAssets.subtitle: After wire insertion, confirm intravascular position with ultrasound visualization in the IJ and cardiac view for right atrial wire tip.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Never dilate or place the catheter without confirmed wire position.

shiftMode: Document pre-block neurovascular status before anesthetizing the digit.
Use small-volume local anesthetic and inject slowly.
Avoid injecting directly through infected tissue when possible.
Aspirate before injection.
Give the block time to work before starting repair.
Reassess anesthesia and distal perfusion before procedure.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Laceration repair
Nailbed injury
Foreign body removal
Paronychia or minor drainage procedure
Fracture or dislocation analgesia adjunct
contraindications: Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Allergy to planned anesthetic
Infection over the injection site, or over the injection path where an alternate approach is available
Major vascular compromise - do not delay urgent surgical evaluation
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
anatomy: Digital nerves run along the medial and lateral aspects of the digit with accompanying vessels.
Injection at the base of the digit can anesthetize both dorsal and volar branches depending on technique.
Avoid circumferential high-volume injection that creates unnecessary tissue pressure.
equipment: Local anesthetic: 1% lidocaine without epinephrine for a short block, or 0.25% bupivacaine when the repair needs hours. Epinephrine in a digit is not the hazard it was taught to be; follow local policy.
3-5 mL syringe
25-30G needle
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; sterile probe cover and gel if using ultrasound
Gauze
Dressing supplies
Procedure tray for definitive repair or drainage
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you inject.
positioning: Position hand or foot comfortably on a stable surface.
Expose the entire digit and remove rings before swelling worsens.
Keep the patient from watching if that increases anxiety.
steps: Confirm digit, injury, and pre-procedure neurovascular status.
Clean injection site.
Insert needle at base of digit along dorsal-lateral aspect depending on the chosen technique.
Aspirate before injection.
Inject slowly while withdrawing or redirecting based on technique.
Repeat on opposite side if needed.
Wait several minutes and test anesthesia.
Proceed with repair, drainage, reduction, or nail procedure once anesthesia is adequate.
confirmation: Patient reports improved pain or numbness in target distribution
Distal perfusion remains intact
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Incomplete anesthesia: wait longer, identify missed distribution, supplement carefully with small volume.
Severe pain with injection: slow down, reposition, buffer/warm anesthetic if available.
Poor perfusion after injection: remove constrictive dressing/rings, reassess volume/epinephrine use, escalate if persistent.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
Nerve irritation or injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity, rare with typical digital block volumes - see the linked rescue card
aftercare: Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure, heat, and biting injury while the block lasts.
Provide wound-specific aftercare.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Digital nerve block for analgesia of the affected digit.
Verbal consent and site confirmation.
Skin prep and clean/sterile injection technique.
Absence of immediate complications.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
seniorPearls: Remove rings early.

visualAssets.title: Digital block injection sites
visualAssets.subtitle: Digital nerves run along the medial and lateral aspects of the digit with accompanying vessels. Injection at the base can reach both dorsal and volar branches depending on technique.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Avoid circumferential high-volume injection - it creates unnecessary tissue pressure in the digit.

agents.note: Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. Lower risk of severe cardiotoxicity than bupivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting - do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: This procedure is when you cannot oxygenate or ventilate your patient.
Call failed airway out loud; assign someone to keep oxygenating while you prep the neck.
Continue passive oxygenation from above throughout procedure, including once cutting starts — leave the facemask or supraglottic device in place and keep delivering.
Ensure full neuromuscular block before you cut — even apneic, a straining patient or closed glottis makes the procedure harder and oxygenation worse.
Landmark before the airway is lost if the airway looks high risk.
Prep wide if time allows — don't let sterile technique delay oxygenation in a true cannot-oxygenate crisis.

One technique: scalpel-bougie-tube (DAS 2025) — number 10 blade, bougie, 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube. A commercial Seldinger kit is a different procedure; if that's what's stocked, follow its instructions instead.
Confirm with ETCO2 and chest rise; secure aggressively.
indications: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate after failed tracheal intubation, supraglottic rescue, and facemask oxygenation.
Failed airway with rapidly worsening hypoxemia
Upper airway obstruction where oral/nasal approach is not feasible
Massive facial trauma or airway contamination when standard approaches fail
contraindications: This technique indicated only for Adult. Pediatric patients < 8-10 years require cannula-based approach due to different anatomy —cricothyroid membrane is small, high, and soft.
Laryngeal fracture or distorted neck anatomy may make landmarks unreliable
Coagulopathy (relative)
anatomy: Cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage.
Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
In obesity or edema, make a generous vertical skin incision first to find the membrane.
equipment: Number 10 scalpel blade, not a pointed 11 or 15 - risk of repeated stabs and posterior wall injury.
Bougie
6.0 cuffed tracheal tube.
Tracheal hook or dilator if available
Suction
BVM with oxygen
Capnography
Securing device/tape
Commercial cricothyrotomy kit
positioning: Supine when possible
Extend the neck fully unless contraindicated; neutral with manual in-line stabilization if cervical spine injury is a concern
Stand at head or side based on access
Expose neck widely
steps: Identify and stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand, and do not let go until the tube is in.
Palpable membrane: transverse stab incision straight through it. Otherwise make an 8-10 cm vertical midline skin incision first, dissect bluntly with a finger down to the larynx, then stab.
Keep the scalpel in the hole and rotate the blade 90 degrees so the sharp edge points towards the feet. It is now the guide for the bougie.
Slide the bougie along the blade, angled towards the feet, into the trachea. Advance 10-15 cm and no further; deeper risks the carina and the posterior tracheal wall.
Remove the scalpel and railroad the 6.0 cuffed tube over the bougie with a gentle twist.
Advance only until the cuff has passed the membrane, then about 1-2 cm more. A 6.0 tube pushed to its usual 21 cm mark sits in the right main bronchus.
Remove the bougie, inflate the cuff, ventilate, and confirm ETCO2 and chest rise.
Secure the tube and reassess oxygenation and ventilation.
ultrasound: Assess membrane palpability before induction whenever a difficult airway is anticipated, and if it is impalpable, locate and mark the membrane with ultrasound before you start.
Do not scan during an established cannot-oxygenate crisis.

visualAssets.title: Safe triangle of insertion
visualAssets.subtitle: Bordered by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line superior to the horizontal level of the nipple, and the apex of the axilla. 4th–5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Insert above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle running along the inferior rib margin.

visualAssets.title: Over-the-rib insertion
visualAssets.subtitle: The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs along the inferior margin of each rib. Always pass the tube over the superior border of the lower rib.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Inferior rib entry risks intercostal artery laceration and hemorrhage.

agents.note: Pleural procedures use a more conservative ceiling than infiltration elsewhere: BTS gives 3 mg/kg to a 250 mg maximum, against the 4.5 mg/kg and 300 mg on the FDA label. Take the lower figure - this is a wide infiltration of skin, periosteum and pleura in a patient who may already be hypoxic.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.
monitoring: Aspirate before each injection; the intercostal vessels sit right where the needle goes.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
Watch for perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, or agitation while infiltrating.

Use ultrasound for fluid; confirm anatomy before puncture.

Pleural effusion requiring drainage

Advance the guidewire while maintaining control. It must pass without impedance - resistance means stop and reassess, never push - and must extend beyond the catheter tip at all times.
Nick the skin and dilate over the wire only to the measured chest-wall depth. Over-insertion of the needle, wire, or dilator can cause life-threatening injury.
Advance catheter over wire; remove wire while maintaining catheter position.
Confirm pigtail formed and side holes intrathoracic.
Connect to drainage system and secure/dress.

shiftMode: This is a temporizing maneuver for suspected tension physiology.
Do not wait for imaging in a crashing patient with compatible findings.
Use a 14 gauge or larger catheter, at least 8 cm (3.25 in) of usable length — a 5 cm catheter often won't reach the pleural space.
Primary site: 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. Alternate: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Failure to decompress is common and expected — have the next step ready before you start.
A failed needle means finger thoracostomy, not another needle.
A tube follows. Not placing one is the exception and needs a reason.
Adult scope only — pediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and aren't covered here.
indications: Suspected tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic or respiratory compromise
Traumatic arrest with decompression pathway
Peri-intubation or ventilated patient crashing with unilateral concern
contraindications: No true contraindication in life-threatening suspected tension physiology
Stable patient with uncertain diagnosis - obtain diagnostic confirmation when possible
Adult scope only. Pediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Enter over the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

The lateral chest wall is thinner than the anterior in most adults, which is why the 4th-5th anterior axillary site is primary. Mind breast tissue and do not go below the nipple line - that is abdomen.
2nd ICS midclavicular can fail in thick chest walls and risks the internal mammary and great vessels if placed too medially; stay at or lateral to the midclavicular line.
equipment: Decompression catheter, 14 gauge or larger with at least 8 cm (3.25 in) usable length, per the stocked device
Chlorhexidine/alcohol if time allows
Gloves
Tape/securement
Chest tube setup ready
positioning: Expose chest rapidly
Arm up if using lateral site and feasible
Do not delay for perfect positioning if peri-arrest
steps: Identify correct side based on clinical scenario.
Site: 4th or 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line; 2nd intercostal space midclavicular as the alternate.
Prep quickly if time allows.
Insert catheter over rib perpendicular to chest wall until pleural entry/air release.
Advance catheter, remove needle, secure.
Reassess immediately, then again within two minutes - a decompressed tension can re-tension on a kinked or occluded catheter - and prepare the definitive thoracostomy.
ultrasound: POCUS can rapidly support diagnosis if it does not delay decompression in a crashing patient.
confirmation: Immediate clinical improvement may occur but is not required.
Reassess BP, oxygenation, breath sounds, ventilator pressures, and chest rise.

A tube follows. The exception is narrow: the original diagnosis was uncertain, the patient is now stable, and ultrasound or chest x-ray shows no or minimal pneumothorax. A rush of air with clinical improvement means there was a pneumothorax under pressure - that patient gets a tube.
troubleshooting: No improvement: wrong side/site, catheter too short, kinked catheter, hemothorax, tamponade, tube problem, or non-thoracic shock.
Catheter occludes: proceed to definitive thoracostomy.
Persistent instability: reassess whole resuscitation, not just the chest.

Failed decompression, tension still plausible: if finger thoracostomy is available to you, do that - it is not length-limited and works where the needle did not. If it is not available, a second needle at the alternate site is reasonable while definitive decompression is arranged.
complications: Misplacement into soft tissue or abdomen
aftercare: Definitive chest tube, unless the narrow stable-and-imaged exception applies.
Imaging once stabilized.
Document rationale for emergent decompression.
documentation: Emergent needle decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax, with the clinical findings.
Site and side.
Catheter placement by anatomic landmarks or local protocol.
Immediate reassessment of response.
Definitive thoracostomy and imaging plan.
seniorPearls: Every successful needle decompression still needs a chest tube.
If the patient is dying and the story fits, decompression is a clinical decision.
Failure is common; reassess immediately.

visualAssets.title: Decompression landmarks
visualAssets.subtitle: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (anterior) or 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (lateral). Lateral approach preferred in muscular or obese patients.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Standard 5 cm catheter may be insufficient in obese patients. Consider longer catheter or finger thoracostomy.

visualAssets.title: Medial danger zone
visualAssets.subtitle: Internal mammary artery runs 1-2 cm lateral to the sternum. Stay in the midclavicular line to avoid it. The intercostal bundle runs along the inferior rib margin.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Too medial risks internal mammary artery. Too low risks abdominal contents.

shiftMode: This is for tamponade physiology, not just an effusion on ultrasound.
Ultrasound picks the pocket and path; subxiphoid landmark route is the fallback for no machine, not the default.
Aortic dissection and post-infarction free-wall rupture are surgical, not needle, problems — read contraindications before needling either.
Have resuscitation, pressors, blood, and surgical backup moving in parallel when indicated.
Advance under visualization if possible; aspirate continuously or frequently.
20-50 mL often reverses tamponade physiology; stopping there is a decision, not a failure.
Keep the obstructive shock differential active — tamponade can coexist with bleeding, tension pneumothorax, or profound hypovolemia.
indications: Cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise
Peri-arrest/arrest with ultrasound evidence of tamponade in appropriate context
Diagnostic/therapeutic drainage when benefits outweigh risks
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening tamponade, with the two exceptions below.

Aortic dissection with hemopericardium: surgical emergency, not a needle. Drainage restores blood pressure and raises the transmural gradient across the tear, converting a contained rupture into an uncontained one.
Post-infarction free-wall rupture: same mechanism. Cardiothoracic surgery now.

Narrow exception for both, per ESC procedural guidance: impending arrest with no immediate surgical option. Drain in small aliquots, of the order of 10-20 mL at a time, targeting the lowest blood pressure that perfuses rather than a normal one, and stop the moment it does. Aliquot size is a local decision.
Purulent effusion or organized clot: a needle and a pigtail will clear neither. Surgical drainage.
Coagulopathy is a caution but may be outweighed by shock.
Adult scope. Pediatric pericardiocentesis differs in needle length, drainage volume, and sedation - not covered here.
anatomy: Choose between subxiphoid, parasternal, and apical by which gives the largest pocket with the shortest safe path.
Parasternal: the internal mammary artery runs close and parallel to the sternal edge. Find it on color Doppler before choosing the spot rather than trusting a distance in centimeters.
Parasternal and apical: enter just above the superior border of the rib below the target space. The intercostal vessels and nerve run along the inferior margin of the rib above.

Subxiphoid has the longest path to the heart and passes closest to the liver. It is the blind fallback: 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, about 30-45 degrees to the skin, aimed at the left shoulder.
Target the fluid pocket. Steer away from the myocardium.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile cover and gel, and color Doppler for the internal mammary and intercostal vessels

Pericardiocentesis kit as stocked by your department - read its IFU in advance. Component sizes, wire diameter, and catheter French vary between sets, and some carry population precautions such as incompletely characterized phthalate exposure in pregnancy, nursing, and children.
If assembling from parts: an 18 gauge thin-wall or spinal needle long enough for the chosen window, a 0.035 inch J-tipped guidewire, a dilator, and a 6-8F pigtail catheter
Three-way stopcock, 20-60 mL syringes, and extension tubing
Closed drainage bag or bottle and a securement dressing if leaving a catheter
Local anesthetic if time allows: 1% lidocaine, a few milliliters for a subxiphoid track in an adult
ECG/monitoring
Sterile pressure tubing or manometry setup, if a transduced waveform is used to confirm the tip is not in the ventricle
Sterile prep/drape/gloves
Resuscitation medications and airway backup
Sample tubes and culture bottles
positioning: Supine, or head up 30-45 degrees if tolerated - elevation moves an effusion anteriorly and inferiorly toward a subxiphoid needle
Expose chest/subxiphoid area widely
Position ultrasound for continuous view
steps: Confirm effusion with tamponade physiology or clinical instability, and confirm this is not dissection or free-wall rupture.
Identify the largest pocket with the shortest safe path. Mark the site and read the depth off the screen before you start.
Prep/drape and anesthetize if time allows.
Advance under real-time visualization, aspirating as you go, watching the tip rather than the hub.
Emergency phase: aspirate only until perfusion returns. 20-50 mL commonly does it. Then stop, re-scan, and decide whether a catheter is needed - do not keep going because fluid keeps coming.
Before dilating over the wire, see the wire inside the pericardial space - no exception, including in an emergency.
Place the catheter with Seldinger control, then confirm the catheter itself - not just the wire - in the pericardial space.
Secure the catheter, attach a closed drainage system, and reassess with ultrasound and hemodynamics.

Drainage after stabilization is staged: keep the initial total under about 500 mL, then drain at intervals rather than continuously. Rapid large-volume removal causes pericardial decompression syndrome.
ultrasound: Choose the largest accessible pocket with the safest path under ultrasound guidance.
Use in-plane visualization when operator skill and window allow.

Uncertain whether the tip is in the pericardium or in a chamber: inject a few milliliters of agitated saline and watch where the bubbles appear. Bubbles in the pericardial space confirm position; bubbles in the right ventricle mean you are inside the heart and must not dilate.
Re-scan after drainage to assess residual fluid and cardiac filling.
confirmation: Improved blood pressure/perfusion
Improved tachycardia or arrest physiology
Ultrasound decrease in effusion and resolution of tamponade findings

Position confirmed rather than inferred. In hemopericardium the aspirate is blood, so its color proves nothing. Use agitated saline, direct visualization of the catheter in the space, or a transduced waveform: a ventricular pressure trace means the catheter is in the ventricle.
Pericardial blood is usually defibrinated and does not clot in the syringe, and brisk clotting suggests intracardiac blood. Treat that as a supporting sign, never as the confirmation.
troubleshooting: No aspirate: reassess window, needle depth, clot, or wrong diagnosis.

Bright pulsatile blood, or blood that clots briskly: stop, do not dilate, and confirm position. If the needle is intracardiac, withdraw it and watch - a needle hole usually seals - then re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion.
Fluid returns but nothing improves: consider clot rather than free fluid, a second loculated pocket, or that tamponade was not the problem. Clot needs surgery.

Collapse after apparently successful drainage: pericardial decompression syndrome. Stop draining, support with fluid and inotropy, and get echo and cardiology. It can appear hours later, so continue watching on the ward.
Recurrent instability: re-scan for reaccumulation, clot, tension pneumothorax, hemorrhage, or obstructive shock alternative.
complications: Right ventricular laceration from dilating or railroading a catheter over a misplaced wire
Internal mammary or intercostal artery injury
Pericardial decompression syndrome: paradoxical hemodynamic collapse, pulmonary edema, or ventricular dysfunction after drainage, typically following rapid or large-volume removal
aftercare: Continuous monitoring and repeat ultrasound.
Watch for decompression syndrome for hours after a large drainage.

Staged drainage after stabilization, with output recorded. Cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery sets the removal target; output below roughly 25-30 mL/day alongside echo showing no significant reaccumulation is the commonly used trigger, and the exact figure is a local plan.
Send fluid as the etiology requires, before the sample is discarded: cell count, culture including mycobacteria, cytology, and protein/LDH as indicated.
Cardiology/cardiothoracic/trauma involvement depending on etiology.
Definitive management of cause.
documentation: Pericardiocentesis for suspected/confirmed tamponade with hemodynamic compromise.
Consent or emergent rationale.
Ultrasound findings, approach, and window.
Position-confirmation method: real-time visualization, agitated saline, or transduced waveform.
Volume and character of fluid, and whether drainage was single-pass or staged.
Residual effusion on post-procedure ultrasound.
Hemodynamic response and complications.
Consultation and ongoing drainage plan.
seniorPearls: The diagnosis is effusion plus tamponade physiology plus patient context, not effusion alone.
Pick the safest window, not the most traditional one.
Small volume out with sudden BP improvement - stop there.
The color of the aspirate answers nothing in trauma - everything there is blood.
If you are reaching for a dilator, you have time to look at the wire.

visualAssets.title: Ultrasound target confirmation
visualAssets.subtitle: Subxiphoid view showing pericardial effusion, myocardium, drainage target, and needle tip entering the fluid pocket.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Confirm the needle tip enters the effusion, not myocardium.

visualAssets.title: Subxiphoid needle geometry (no-ultrasound fallback)
visualAssets.subtitle: Blind fallback route only, for when no machine is available. Needle enters 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, tracks shallowly under the costal margin at about 30-45 degrees, and aims toward the left shoulder.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: With ultrasound available, the safest pocket sets the trajectory, not this geometry. Steep or deep trajectories risk myocardium or liver.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Use when unstable bradycardia is not responding or needs bridge therapy.
Keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors running while placing, if unstable.
Know the generator before you need it — rate, output in mA, sensitivity, battery, and which cable mates it to this catheter.
Electrical capture is not enough — confirm mechanical capture with pulse/BP/arterial waveform.
Spikes with no capture at maximum output: reposition rather than increasing output.
Secure catheter and generator carefully; dislodgement is common.
Do not remove backup pads or pressors until capture is reliable and the catheter is secured.
indications: Unstable bradycardia refractory to medications/transcutaneous pacing
High-grade AV block with instability
Reversible bradycardia - drug toxicity, hyperkalemia, Lyme carditis, myocarditis - where pacing bridges to resolution
Bridge to permanent pacing or definitive management
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening bradycardia
Prosthetic tricuspid valve - a pacing lead cannot be floated across a mechanical tricuspid
Severe agitation may require sedation/airway planning
Infection or thrombus at access site affects site selection
Adult scope.
anatomy: Right internal jugular is the preferred route.
Left subclavian is the second choice for a longer dwell. Avoid an intrathoracic subclavian puncture - it risks pneumothorax and it compromises the vein a permanent device may need.
Femoral works and is sometimes the only option, but it carries higher infection and thrombosis rates and loses capture with leg movement.
Preserve the side planned for the permanent pacemaker.
The balloon-tipped catheter floats with blood flow toward the RV when advanced correctly. From the right internal jugular the right ventricle is typically at about 30-35 cm.
ECG changes and capture help guide placement.
equipment: Central venous introducer sized to this pacing catheter
Balloon-tipped pacing catheter with its sterile contamination sleeve and locking mechanism
Pacing generator with battery checked, and the specific connector cable that mates it to this catheter
A syringe of air for the balloon - air only, never fluid or contrast

Monitor/defib pads
Ultrasound for venous access
Flushes
Suture/securement
Pressors and transcutaneous pacing available
positioning: Supine
Sterile central line position based on chosen access site
Defib pads on patient
steps: Obtain central venous access and place the introducer.
Test the balloon before it goes in, then connect the pacing catheter to the generator and confirm it paces.
Set the generator before insertion: rate about 60-80 or above the patient's own rate, output high to start at around 5-10 mA, and the mode the rhythm calls for.
Inflate the balloon, typically 1.0-1.5 mL of air.
Advance gently while watching the ECG for ectopy and capture. Never advance against resistance, and never advance or withdraw with the balloon inflated against resistance.
Capture, then find the threshold: reduce the output until capture is lost, note that number, and set the output at two to three times it.
Confirm mechanical capture with pulse, blood pressure, or arterial waveform.
Deflate the balloon, secure the catheter and the generator, and obtain a chest radiograph for position, depth, and pneumothorax.
Record rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth.
ultrasound: Ultrasound helps obtain venous access and may help assess catheter course/complications.
confirmation: Electrical capture on ECG
Mechanical capture with palpable pulse/BP/arterial waveform
Improved perfusion/mental status
Chest x-ray for catheter position, depth, and complications
troubleshooting: No capture at maximum output: position, not power. Deflate, withdraw a few centimeters, reinflate, and refloat. Keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors going while you do.
Intermittent capture: secure, reposition, increase output margin.
Threshold rising over hours: the catheter is migrating or the tip is becoming inflamed. Recheck position and securement, and hand that number over to the next team.
Ventricular ectopy: withdraw/reposition if irritating myocardium.
Sudden hypotension after a good capture: think right ventricular perforation and tamponade. Scan.
Hypotension despite capture: reassess rate, shock, medications, and mechanical complications.
Diaphragmatic pacing or hiccups: the tip is against the diaphragmatic surface or through the wall. Reassess position.
complications: Bleeding or hematoma at the access site
aftercare: Continuous monitoring.
Cardiology/ICU admission
Review the need every day and document the plan. Dwell time drives infection, thrombosis, and displacement
Repeat capture checks after movement/transport.
Keep transcutaneous pacing capability and pressors immediately available for the whole dwell.
Secure generator and catheter to prevent accidental migration.
documentation: Transvenous pacemaker for unstable bradycardia or conduction disease.
Consent or emergent rationale.
Venous access site and technique, and the reason that site was chosen.
Catheter, generator, and connector cable by name.
Rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth at capture.
Mechanical capture confirmed clinically or hemodynamically.
Securement, imaging, dwell-time plan, and consultation.
seniorPearls: Air in the balloon. Not saline, not contrast.
Write the threshold down.
Keep pads on until the whole setup is stable and secured.
Every movement can lose capture; check after transport.
Spikes without capture at maximum output are a malposition, not a generator problem.

visualAssets.subtitle: From the right internal jugular the right ventricle is typically at about 30-35 cm. Electrical capture on the ECG and mechanical capture at the pulse are separate checks.

shiftMode: Staff and equip this as an airway procedure, not a comfort procedure.
Adult moderate-to-deep sedation, ED or ICU only — not general anesthesia, elective or outpatient sedation, or pediatric sedation; each has different staffing, monitoring, fasting, and recovery rules.
Sedation is a continuum and the patient can go deeper than intended. Staff and equip to rescue one level deeper than the target.
A dedicated clinician monitors and does nothing else — the proceduralist can't do it; hands and eyes are on the procedure.
Pre-brief airway risk, hemodynamics, meds, dose plan, and rescue plan.

Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring, cycled blood pressure, and continuous waveform capnography — capnography is required, not optional. On supplemental oxygen, saturation lags true oxygenation by minutes.
Have suction, BVM, airway adjuncts, and reversal/rescue meds physically in the room.
Do not give more medication because the room is impatient; dose to patient response.
indications: Painful or anxiety-provoking procedure requiring controlled sedation
Reduction, cardioversion, abscess drainage, chest tube, complex wound care
Facilitation of urgent imaging/procedure when benefits outweigh risk
contraindications: High aspiration risk, difficult airway, severe physiologic instability, or inadequate staffing/equipment are major cautions
Agent-specific contraindications depend on medication and patient physiology
Urgent sedation is not delayed for fasting time.

Elective sedation is a different decision. Full-stomach risk - bowel obstruction, active vomiting, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, late pregnancy, obtundation, gastroparesis, or a GLP-1 receptor agonist - changes depth, agent, airway plan, or whether to sedate at all, not the hours waited.
Adult scope only. Pediatric sedation - different agents and routes, different monitoring intervals, different discharge rules - is not covered by this card.
anatomy: Airway patency, respiratory drive, and hemodynamic reserve.
Know whether the patient will be supine, lateral, or immobilized during the procedure.
equipment: Cardiac monitor, pulse oximeter, BP cycling
Continuous waveform capnography
Oxygen source and nasal cannula/NRB
BVM with mask and PEEP valve if available
Suction connected
Oral/nasal airways
Advanced airway equipment immediately available
Sedative/analgesic medications labeled
Naloxone and flumazenil available - see the procedural sedation apnea rescue card for doses.
IV access
Procedure equipment ready before sedation
positioning: Position for airway access and procedure success
Preoxygenate when risk is meaningful
Remove loose dentures/foreign bodies if appropriate
steps: Assess the indication, comorbidities, allergies, and ASA-style risk, and assess the airway specifically: mouth opening, thyromental distance, neck movement, obesity, beard, obstructive sleep apnea, and any previous difficult airway.
Obtain consent and perform time-out.
Assign sedation monitor and proceduralist roles.
Prepare airway/rescue equipment before medications.

If the procedure also involves infiltration or a block, calculate the maximum local anesthetic dose before you start. Sedation does not change the maximum, and a sedated patient cannot report early toxicity.
Administer medication incrementally and wait for peak effect before redosing.
Continuously monitor ventilation, oxygenation, perfusion, and procedural conditions.
Treat airway obstruction/apnea immediately.
Observe until patient returns to appropriate baseline and discharge/admission criteria met.
confirmation: Adequate procedure conditions
Ventilation maintained by ETCO2/chest rise
Oxygenation maintained
Hemodynamics acceptable
Return to baseline mental status/airway function before discharge
troubleshooting: Apnea: stop dosing, jaw thrust, suction, airway adjunct, BVM/PEEP, prepare intubation.

Laryngospasm: stridor, or silent obstruction with paradoxical chest movement. Remove the stimulus, 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask with jaw thrust and CPAP-level pressure, then subparalyzing succinylcholine if it does not break. See the laryngospasm rescue card for doses.
Vomiting: head down and turned to the side, suction under direct vision, stop the procedure. Do not blindly instrument the airway.
Hypotension: stop sedative, fluids/pressors, reassess bleeding/sepsis/agent effect.
Emergence/agitation: reduce stimulation, protect patient, consider agent-specific management.
Inadequate sedation: pause procedure, reassess analgesia vs sedation, redose deliberately.
aftercare: Recover in a monitored area with the monitoring used during sedation; reassess at defined intervals.
Discharge criteria, all of them: back to baseline mental status, protecting their own airway, vital signs at baseline, pain controlled, and moving at their usual level.
After naloxone or flumazenil, extend the observation period. Both wear off before the drug they reversed - roughly a two-hour window in which resedation can occur.
Document pre/post assessment, meds/doses/times, monitoring, complications, and recovery status.
Written discharge precautions and a responsible adult if outpatient: no driving, machinery, alcohol, or important decisions for 24 hours.
documentation: Procedural sedation to facilitate the documented procedure.
Consent obtained; risks/benefits discussed when feasible.
Monitoring: cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, continuous waveform capnography.
Sedation medications, doses, and times in MAR/procedure record.
Tolerance of sedation; airway and hemodynamic events with interventions.
Recovery to appropriate baseline before disposition.
seniorPearls: Do not let the procedure start before the room is ready.
ETCO2 buys time; pulse ox tells you late.
Choose the sedative you know how to rescue from.

medicationDosing.indication: Adult procedural sedation. Doses are targets titrated to effect, not ceilings, and are lower than the induction doses on the intubation card.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Be able to rescue a patient one level deeper than you intend. Propofol and dissociative-dose ketamine can both produce general anesthesia, so the room must be staffed and equipped to manage an apneic, unprotected airway before the first milliliter goes in.

medications.caution: Give over 1-2 minutes; a rapid push causes apnea. Dissociation is all or nothing, so an underdose does not give light sedation - it gives an agitated, undissociated patient. Increases secretions and is the agent most associated with laryngospasm: have suction in hand. No reversal agent exists. Intramuscular 4-5 mg/kg is an option without IV access, with slower onset and longer recovery.

medications.durationNote: lasts 5-10 min; redose 0.25-0.5 mg/kg every 1-3 min
medications.caution: Apnea and hypotension are expected effects at these doses, not complications. No analgesia - pair it with an analgesic for a painful procedure. Dose on lean body weight and reduce it in the elderly or hypovolemic.

This is roughly half the intubation induction dose in this app - check which card you are reading. Myoclonus is common and can be mistaken for a seizure or for inadequate sedation; treating it with more etomidate is the wrong move.
Slow to peak. Wait the full 2-5 minutes before redosing or you will stack doses. Synergistic with opioids for apnea: reduce both when they are combined.
Analgesia, not sedation. Combined with any sedative the risk of apnea is more than additive, so reduce both. Chest wall rigidity is rare but occurs with rapid high-dose administration.

selectionGuidance: Brief and painful, hemodynamics uncertain: ketamine.
Brief and not painful, patient stable: propofol.
Painful, and you want analgesia separate from sedation: an opioid plus a reduced dose of a sedative.
Hemodynamically fragile and sedation is unavoidable: etomidate at the sedation dose above.
Anxiolysis only, with no procedural pain: midazolam alone.
medicationDosing.sourceNote: Conventional adult emergency-department sedation doses, accepted by the clinical owner on 2026-07-30. The ASA and ACEP guidelines in this record's references govern staffing, monitoring, depth, and fasting rather than specific doses; the figures here are widely used starting points for titration in a monitored patient, not a protocol, and are not independently verified against a primary pharmacology source. Paediatric sedation is out of scope for this card.

shiftMode: Suspected bacterial meningitis: antibiotics first — nothing about the LP (imaging, positioning, consent, finding tubes) is allowed to delay the first dose.
Draw blood cultures before antibiotics, not the LP — an LP after antibiotics still answers the question (cell count, glucose, protein, and PCR survive the first dose); culture is what may be lost.
Check blood glucose immediately before the LP when meningitis is suspected — the CSF:blood glucose ratio needs a paired value, not this morning's.
Position is the procedure: poor flexion and rotation kill success.
Use L3-L4 or L4-L5; avoid going too high.
Atraumatic pencil-point needle is the default; it needs an introducer.
Have tubes labeled and the manometer assembled before puncture if opening pressure is needed.
If traumatic or no flow, pause and reposition rather than digging.
Document the neurological examination before local anesthetic when feasible.
indications: Concern for meningitis or encephalitis
Subarachnoid hemorrhage evaluation after a negative CT taken outside the window in which CT alone is sufficient
Measurement of opening pressure
Diagnostic CSF studies for inflammatory, malignant, or infectious etiologies
Therapeutic CSF removal where that is the agreed plan, as in idiopathic intracranial hypertension
contraindications: Image the head first, and treat first, if any of these are present: focal neurological deficit, new-onset seizure, a reduced or fluctuating conscious level, papilledema, abnormal pupils, abnormal posturing, or significant immunocompromise. These features make a mass lesion or impending herniation likely; a routine CT for everyone is not indicated.
Deferring the LP for imaging never defers the antibiotics.
Stabilize first and LP later in shock, respiratory compromise, or uncontrolled seizures. The positioning alone can be lethal in a marginal patient.

Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or therapeutic anticoagulation: neuraxial procedure, concealed bleed. Follow a named local antithrombotic policy - the hold interval depends on the agent, the dose, renal function, and how urgent the LP is. A coagulopathy that defers the LP still does not defer antibiotics.
Overlying infection at puncture site
Unstable patient who cannot tolerate positioning
Adult scope. Pediatric and neonatal LP differ in interspace, needle length, sedation, CSF volume, and opening-pressure interpretation - not covered here.
anatomy: Use line between iliac crests approximating L4 spinous process.
Tuffier's line is an approximation and sits higher than expected in obesity and in pregnancy. If the level matters, count up from the sacrum or mark the interspace with ultrasound.
Needle enters midline between spinous processes toward umbilicus.
Conus usually ends above adult L3; use lower lumbar spaces.
equipment: LP tray
Sterile gloves, surgical mask, prep, and drape
Atraumatic pencil-point spinal needle, 22-25 gauge, with its introducer - the default for adults
Cutting (Quincke) needle as the fallback when no atraumatic needle is stocked
A longer needle available for large body habitus
Manometer and three-way tap if opening pressure is needed
Collection tubes labeled 1-4
1% lidocaine and a small needle for skin and deeper infiltration
Bandage
Assistant for positioning
positioning: Lateral decubitus for opening pressure; hips and neck flexed but the airway comfortable
Sitting-flexed improves success and midline identification but makes opening pressure uninterpretable. If you need a pressure, you need lateral.
Shoulders and hips perpendicular to bed, with the plane of the back vertical rather than rolled
Once the needle is in and before measuring, let the legs come down. Flexion falsely raises the opening pressure.
steps: Suspected meningitis: blood cultures, then antibiotics, then everything below.
Review contraindications and the imaging criteria, consent, and required studies.
Position patient carefully, identify the interspace, and mark it.
Prep/drape sterile field.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue.
Insert the introducer, then the atraumatic needle through it, angled slightly cephalad. Bevel orientation is a cutting-needle instruction and does not apply to a pencil-point needle.
Advance slowly. An atraumatic needle gives a subtle or absent pop - check for flow every few millimeters by removing the stylet.
Measure opening pressure before removing any CSF: lateral position, legs and neck relaxed, manometer zeroed at the interspace.
Collect CSF in ordered tubes.
Replace stylet before removing needle; dress site and reassess the neurological examination.
ultrasound: Ultrasound can help identify midline and depth in obese or difficult anatomy but does not replace sterile technique.
Most useful before the first attempt, as a marking tool.
confirmation: CSF obtained and sent for ordered studies
Opening pressure measured before CSF removal, with the position, leg position, and zero reference recorded beside the number. A commonly cited adult range is about 6-25 cmH2O.
Straining, coughing, Valsalva, hypercapnia, and a flexed position all raise it. A single high number in a struggling patient is not intracranial hypertension.
Patient neurologic status reassessed
Tube numbers and appearance documented
troubleshooting: No CSF: recheck positioning, level, angle, depth; consider longer needle or ultrasound marking.
Bone repeatedly: withdraw to subcutaneous tissue and redirect cephalad slightly.
Flow starts then stops: rotate the needle 90 degrees. A nerve root or the arachnoid can occlude the aperture; rotate rather than advance.
Traumatic tap: minimize needle movement; consider another level if needed.
Post-LP headache: counsel, fluids/analgesia, blood patch pathway if persistent/severe.
aftercare: Bed rest does not prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Lying flat may make an established one more tolerable; do not offer it as prophylaxis.
Send CSF promptly with correct labels and orders.
Reassess neuro status and puncture site.

New or worsening back pain, leg weakness, numbness, or urinary retention after an LP is a spinal or epidural hematoma until proven otherwise. Urgent MRI and a neurosurgical conversation - not analgesia and reassurance. The risk is highest in anticoagulated or coagulopathic patients, and the window in which decompression preserves function is hours.
Give return precautions for severe headache, fever, weakness, urinary retention, or site issues.
documentation: Lumbar puncture indication.
Consent; contraindications and imaging criteria reviewed as appropriate.
Suspected meningitis: time of blood cultures, time of first antibiotic dose, and time of LP.
Position and sterile technique.
Needle type and gauge - atraumatic or cutting - and the level of insertion.
CSF obtained, or unsuccessful attempts.
Opening pressure with position, leg position, and zero reference, if measured.
CSF appearance, tubes, and studies; tolerance and complications.
seniorPearls: Most failed LPs are positioning failures, not needle failures.
Do not chase bone deeper and deeper; reset your angle.
Label tubes before you are holding CSF.
The atraumatic needle has no satisfying pop. Check for flow.

visualAssets.clinicalWarning: If bone is hit, withdraw and redirect — do not force through.
