visualAssets.title: Short-axis probe positioning
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe perpendicular to the target vein. Vein appears as a round anechoic compressible structure. Artery is pulsatile and non-compressible.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Compress to distinguish vein from artery before needle entry.

visualAssets.title: Needle tip visualization
visualAssets.subtitle: Track the needle tip as a hyperechoic dot entering the vein lumen. Tenting of the anterior wall confirms contact. Flash in the catheter hub confirms intraluminal position.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Always visualize the needle tip, not just the shaft. Shaft visualization can be deceptive about true tip location.

shiftMode: This is a vision-saving, time-critical procedure — do not wait for ophthalmology or imaging if the diagnosis is clear.
Diagnose clinically: acute orbital compartment syndrome with a tense, proptotic eye, decreased vision/APD, raised intraocular pressure, and pain after trauma or retrobulbar hemorrhage.
The goal is to release the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (cantholysis) — the canthotomy incision alone is not enough.
Anesthetize and clamp the lateral canthus to reduce bleeding, then cut horizontally to the orbital rim.
Strum for the inferior crus and cut it; the lower lid should swing free and the globe should soften.
Reassess intraocular pressure and proptosis; if still tense, release the superior crus as well.
Do not let lack of an ophthalmologist delay the release in a clear orbital compartment syndrome.
indications: Acute orbital compartment syndrome (commonly from retrobulbar hemorrhage) with vision threat
Markedly raised intraocular pressure with a tense, proptotic globe and an afferent pupillary defect
Progressive vision loss with orbital tension after facial/orbital trauma or surgery
contraindications: Suspected globe rupture - manipulating the orbit can extrude intraocular contents; avoid and get emergent ophthalmology
No evidence of orbital compartment syndrome
An alternative, immediately treatable cause of the findings that does not involve orbital pressure
anatomy: The lateral canthal tendon anchors the eyelids to the orbital rim and has a superior and an inferior crus.
Cantholysis of the inferior crus releases the lower lid and decompresses the orbit; both crura may need release.
The orbital septum and retrobulbar space hold the hemorrhage that raises pressure on the optic nerve and its blood supply.
The lacrimal apparatus sits medially; the lateral approach avoids it. Aim toward the lateral orbital rim, away from the globe.
equipment: Local anesthetic with epinephrine: 1-2 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, a small syringe, and a 25-27G needle
Straight hemostat
Blunt-tipped scissors - Stevens tenotomy or blunt Westcott. Not iris or sharp straight scissors.
Toothed forceps
Gauze and saline for hemostasis and visualization
Tonometer to measure intraocular pressure if available
Eye protection/sterile gloves
Good lighting or headlamp
positioning: Patient supine with the head stabilized and the affected eye fully accessible.
Optimize lighting directly on the lateral canthus.
Have an assistant help retract the lids and manage bleeding if available.
Position yourself at the side of the affected eye for a horizontal lateral approach.
steps: Confirm orbital compartment syndrome clinically and exclude obvious globe rupture.
Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine into the lateral canthus toward the lateral orbital rim.
Clamp the lateral canthus horizontally with a hemostat for 1-2 minutes to crush tissue and reduce bleeding.
Remove the hemostat and make a horizontal canthotomy incision through the crushed tissue to the lateral orbital rim (about 1-2 cm).
Pull the lower lid outward and downward with forceps to put the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon on tension.

Strum and identify the taut inferior crus, then cut it with the blunt scissors directed toward the orbital rim - inferiorly and slightly posteriorly, away from the globe. The lower lid should release and the globe soften.
Confirm the inferior release is complete before anything else. The lid should swing freely away from the globe; if it does not, there is still tendon to cut - cut it rather than moving superior.
Reassess: intraocular pressure, visual acuity or at least light perception, the pupil, and orbital tension.

Release the superior crus only if all of these are true after a complete inferior cantholysis: the orbit is still tense, the intraocular pressure is still raised, and vision or the pupil has not improved. Superior release adds lacrimal artery and gland risk.
Control bleeding with gentle pressure and arrange emergent ophthalmology evaluation.
confirmation: Lower lid swings free after inferior cantholysis
Globe is visibly softer and proptosis reduced
Measured intraocular pressure has fallen toward normal if a tonometer is available
Improvement (or halted deterioration) in vision and pupillary findings
Hemostasis achieved at the canthotomy site
troubleshooting: No softening after the incision: the canthotomy cut alone is insufficient - perform the cantholysis.
Still tense after inferior cantholysis: confirm the release was complete before going superior.
Cannot identify the crus: pull the lid on tension and strum for the taut band toward the orbital rim before cutting.
Brisk bleeding obscuring the field: apply gentle pressure and use the pre-incision hemostat clamp to limit it.
Suspect globe rupture mid-procedure: stop manipulating the globe and get emergent ophthalmology.
complications: Iatrogenic globe injury if the cut strays toward the globe
Incomplete decompression from canthotomy without cantholysis
Scarring or lid malposition after repair
Failure to restore vision if decompression is delayed
aftercare: Arrange emergent ophthalmology evaluation and definitive management.
Continue measures to lower intraocular pressure per ophthalmology guidance.
Serially reassess vision, pupil, and orbital tension until specialist care assumes the patient.
Document the time of decompression relative to symptom onset.
documentation: Lateral canthotomy and inferior (with or without superior) cantholysis performed for acute orbital compartment syndrome.
Clinical findings: proptosis, intraocular pressure with the value, visual acuity or best available assessment, and pupillary findings including relative afferent pupillary defect.
Both eyes documented - the unaffected eye is the baseline.
Vision or pupil not assessable (intubated, obtunded, lids too swollen) recorded as not testable, not left blank.
Globe rupture not suspected prior to the procedure.
Inferior crus released with resultant lid release and globe softening; whether the superior crus was released, and the findings that justified it.
Post-procedure intraocular pressure, vision, and pupillary findings recorded, with the times.
Emergent ophthalmology consultation arranged; time from onset to decompression documented.
seniorPearls: The canthotomy is the approach; the cantholysis is the treatment. Cutting skin without releasing the crus does nothing for the pressure.
Cut now, consult after. Sight is lost in tens of minutes of optic nerve ischemia.
If the globe might be ruptured, stop - decompression can extrude a salvageable eye.
references: U.S. Joint Trauma System. Eye Trauma: Initial Care Clinical Practice Guideline. 2021. https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Eye_Trauma_Initial_Care_01_Jun_2021_ID03.pdf
American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki. Orbital Compartment Syndrome. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Orbital_Compartment_Syndrome
Institutional ophthalmic emergency protocols; verify local consultation pathway and which blunt scissors are stocked on the eye tray.

visualAssets.title: Inferior crus release
visualAssets.subtitle: The lateral canthal tendon has a superior and an inferior crus; the cantholysis target is the inferior crus at the orbital rim.
visualAssets.caption: Cut the inferior crus at the lateral canthus, angling away from the globe toward the orbital rim.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Aim toward the lateral orbital rim, away from the globe.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Assess the wound for foreign body, tendon/nerve/vessel injury, joint involvement, and contamination before closing anything.
Check distal neurovascular and motor function and document it before infiltrating anesthetic.
Anesthetize, then explore through the full depth and range of motion — injuries hide off the resting position.
Irrigate copiously with normal saline or potable tap water; pressure and volume matter more than additives.
Choose closure: primary now, delayed primary for high-contamination/older wounds, or referral for complex/specialty areas.
Approximate without tension; evert edges; match suture size to location and remove on schedule.
Update tetanus and document wound, exploration, repair, and aftercare.
indications: Acute traumatic laceration amenable to primary closure
Wound where closure improves hemostasis, function, or cosmesis
Clean or cleanable wound within an appropriate time window for the location
contraindications: Signs of established infection (close only after treatment, or use delayed primary closure)
Heavily contaminated or bite wounds in high-risk locations (consider delayed closure or specialty input)
Wounds with retained foreign material not yet removed
Injuries needing operative or specialist repair (tendon, nerve, artery, open fracture, complex facial/eyelid)
Wounds beyond a safe time window for the body region and contamination level
anatomy: Know the underlying structures at the site: tendons, nerves, vessels, ducts, and joints near the wound.
Facial landmarks (vermilion border, eyelid margins, eyebrow) require precise alignment and often specialty care.
Skin tension lines guide orientation and influence scarring.
Depth determines whether deep dermal sutures are needed to close dead space and reduce tension.
equipment: Local anesthetic: 1% or 2% lidocaine, with epinephrine unless local policy excludes it for this field. Calculate the ceiling on this card before drawing up.
Syringe and small-gauge needle for infiltration
Irrigation: normal saline or potable water, large syringe with splash guard
Skin antiseptic and sterile drape
Suture material appropriate to location (e.g., 6-0 face, 4-0/5-0 extremities, deeper absorbable for dermis)
Needle driver, toothed forceps, suture scissors, and a sterile suture tray
Sterile gloves and good lighting
Wound dressing
Tetanus-diphtheria vaccine and tetanus immune globulin, both obtainable in the department
positioning: Position the patient and the wound for direct visualization and ergonomic access.
Optimize lighting; use a headlamp or task light for deep or angled wounds.
Support the limb or area so the patient can hold still during repair.
Examine the wound through its full range of motion to detect deep injuries.
steps: Obtain history including mechanism, timing, contamination, and tetanus immunization history - the number of prior doses, not just the date of the last one.
Document distal neurovascular and motor function before anesthesia.
Infiltrate local anesthetic and confirm adequate analgesia.
Explore the full wound depth and range of motion for foreign body or deep-structure injury.
Irrigate copiously with saline or potable water under moderate pressure.
Achieve hemostasis and debride devitalized tissue conservatively.
Place deep dermal absorbable sutures if needed to reduce tension and close dead space.
Approximate the skin edges with everting interrupted sutures, matching size and spacing to the location.
Confirm edge apposition and eversion without tension or gaping.
Classify the wound and make the tetanus decision explicitly - see aftercare - then apply the dressing and give wound-care and suture-removal instructions.
ultrasound: Ultrasound can help localize radiolucent foreign bodies (wood, plastic) not seen on x-ray.
Useful to confirm or exclude retained material before closure when suspicion is high.
Can assess depth and proximity to vessels or tendons in selected wounds.
confirmation: Wound explored and free of foreign body and unrepaired deep injury
Adequate irrigation performed
Edges approximated and everted without tension
Hemostasis achieved
Tetanus status addressed and aftercare instructions given
troubleshooting: Persistent bleeding: direct pressure, identify and control the source; avoid blind deep ties near nerves.
Edges will not approximate without tension: place deep dermal sutures or consider undermining; reassess closure choice.
Inadequate anesthesia: supplement infiltration or use a regional/field block; buffer lidocaine to reduce sting.
Wound edge necrosis or contamination concern: consider delayed primary closure instead of forcing primary repair.
Suspected tendon/nerve injury found on exploration: do not close over it blindly; involve the appropriate specialist.
aftercare: Keep the wound clean and dry per local guidance; instruct on signs of infection.
Provide a suture-removal timeline appropriate to the body region.

Classify the wound first: clean and minor, or dirty and major - contaminated with dirt, feces, or saliva, a puncture, an avulsion, or a wound from a missile, crush, burn, or frostbite. Then count the patient's prior tetanus doses.

Three or more prior doses: give a tetanus-containing vaccine if the last dose was 10 or more years ago for a clean minor wound, or 5 or more years ago for a dirty or major wound. No immune globulin either way.
Fewer than three prior doses, or an unknown history: give the vaccine for any wound, and add tetanus immune globulin 250 IU intramuscularly for a dirty or major wound.
HIV infection or severe immunodeficiency with a dirty or major wound: give immune globulin regardless of the vaccination history, because the vaccine response cannot be relied on.
Give the vaccine and the immune globulin with separate syringes at separate sites.
Arrange follow-up or wound check for higher-risk wounds and consider antibiotics only when indicated.
documentation: Laceration repaired at [site]; mechanism and timing recorded.
Pre-repair distal neurovascular and motor exam documented as intact.
Wound explored; no retained foreign body or deep-structure injury identified (or findings noted).
Irrigation performed; closure type and suture material/size documented.
Local anesthetic agent, concentration, and total volume recorded.
Wound classified as clean-minor or dirty-major, prior tetanus dose count recorded, and the vaccine and immune globulin decision documented with what was given.
Aftercare and suture-removal instructions provided.
seniorPearls: Explore before you close.
Examine the wound in the position of injury, not the position of rest; tendon lacerations retract.
Eversion and tension control determine the scar.
references: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus. 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html
Food and Drug Administration. Xylocaine and Xylocaine with epinephrine prescribing information. 2024. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/006488Orig1s100lbl.pdf
Institutional wound-care and antibiotic-prophylaxis policies; verify local guidance and that tetanus immune globulin is stocked where you work.

visualAssets.title: Everting interrupted suture
visualAssets.subtitle: Needle entry angle and bite depth set the edge eversion that gives a tension-free closure.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Close without tension - evert the edges, and use deep dermal sutures where the depth requires them.

shiftMode: Confirm anterior dislocation and document neurovascular status - especially axillary nerve sensation over the deltoid - before and after.
Neurovascular compromise means reduce sooner, not wait — the humeral head causing it is fixed by reduction. Call the specialist in parallel, not first.
Get pre-reduction imaging unless the presentation is clearly recurrent and atraumatic per local practice.
Optimize analgesia/relaxation: intra-articular block, procedural sedation, or a gentle technique the patient can tolerate.
Choose a low-force technique first (scapular manipulation, Cunningham, external rotation) before high-traction methods.
Reduce slowly and steadily; pain and muscle spasm fight speed, not patience.
Confirm reduction clinically and with post-reduction imaging; recheck neurovascular status.
Immobilize and arrange orthopedic follow-up.
indications: Acute anterior glenohumeral dislocation
Dislocation with axillary nerve deficit
Dislocation with a pulseless or ischemic limb - reduce urgently while vascular surgery is called, do not wait for them to arrive
Recurrent dislocation appropriate for ED reduction
contraindications: Associated displaced fracture that warrants orthopedic reduction (e.g., certain surgical-neck fractures) - traction can displace the head further
Posterior or inferior dislocation requiring a different, specific approach
Open dislocation - theater, not the resus bay
Inability to safely provide analgesia/sedation when required
Neurovascular compromise is not a contraindication - see indications and troubleshooting for the sequence.
anatomy: The glenohumeral joint trades stability for mobility; the humeral head sits anterior/inferior in the common dislocation.
The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck of the humerus and is the most commonly injured nerve — test deltoid sensation and function.
The brachial plexus and axillary vessels lie medially; assess distal pulses and perfusion.
Associated injuries include Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions and greater tuberosity fractures.
equipment: Stretcher or bed allowing the chosen technique and patient positioning
Monitoring and supplies for procedural sedation if used, per the procedural sedation card (pulse oximetry, capnography, oxygen, airway kit)
Intra-articular block: 20 mL of 1% lidocaine, a 20 mL syringe, and a 21G needle, with full sterile prep
A sheet for counter-traction if a traction technique is chosen
Sling or shoulder immobilizer for post-reduction
Imaging access for pre- and post-reduction films
positioning: Scapular manipulation: patient prone or seated, affected arm hanging with gentle traction.
Cunningham/external rotation: patient seated upright, elbow adducted to the side.
Traction-counter-traction: patient supine with a sheet around the torso for counter-traction.
Choose the position that matches your technique and the patient's tolerance and comfort.
steps: Confirm the diagnosis and document a detailed neurovascular exam including axillary nerve function.
If the limb is pulseless or ischemic: call vascular surgery and reduce now. Do not sequence those.
Obtain pre-reduction imaging unless clearly indicated otherwise by local protocol.
Provide analgesia/relaxation: intra-articular block, procedural sedation, or a sedation-sparing gentle technique.

Intra-articular block, if used: sterile prep, enter from the lateral or posterior approach into the joint, aspirate, and inject. 20 mL of 1% lidocaine is 200 mg - check the dose calculator on this card before adding any other local anesthetic.
Select a first-line low-force technique (scapular manipulation, Cunningham, or external rotation).
Apply slow, steady force appropriate to the technique, allowing muscle relaxation over time.
Feel or observe for the humeral head relocating into the glenoid.
If unsuccessful, optimize analgesia and try an alternative technique rather than escalating force abruptly.
Confirm reduction clinically (restored contour and motion) and recheck neurovascular status.
Obtain post-reduction imaging to confirm position and assess for fracture.
Immobilize in a sling/immobilizer and arrange orthopedic follow-up.
ultrasound: Bedside ultrasound (posterior approach) can confirm dislocation and successful reduction in real time.
Useful to reduce repeat radiographs and to guide intra-articular block placement.
Can assist confirming relocation before formal post-reduction films.
confirmation: Palpable/visible relocation of the humeral head with restored shoulder contour
Improved range of motion and reduced pain after reduction
Intact post-reduction neurovascular exam (including axillary nerve)
Post-reduction imaging confirms congruent joint and no new fracture
Shoulder immobilized and follow-up arranged
troubleshooting: Pulseless or cold limb: reduce urgently and call vascular surgery in parallel. Reassess the pulse the moment the head relocates. A pulse that does not return after reduction is an arterial injury until imaging says otherwise. Axillary artery injury is commonest in the elderly.
Reduction failing: optimize analgesia and relaxation - add an intra-articular block or sedation and switch technique.
Persistent inability after multiple attempts: reassess for fracture or alternate dislocation type and involve orthopedics.

New neurologic deficit after reduction: document and arrange urgent orthopedic/neuro evaluation. A deficit present before reduction and unchanged after it is usually a traction injury to the axillary nerve and usually recovers.
Suspected associated fracture on pre-reduction film: weigh technique choice and consult orthopedics.
Severe pain limiting any technique: optimize analgesia before continuing rather than forcing traction.
complications: Rotator cuff injury, especially in older patients
Sedation-related complications when procedural sedation is used
aftercare: Immobilize in a sling or shoulder immobilizer for one to three weeks; shorter is generally preferred.

First-time dislocation under about 25: high recurrence rate - arrange orthopedic assessment for whether stabilization is indicated. Over about 40: suspect an associated rotator cuff tear and arrange assessment for that instead - persistent weakness is a cuff tear until examined.
Start early range-of-motion within the limits orthopedics set.
Provide analgesia and instructions to avoid provocative positions - abduction with external rotation.
Arrange orthopedic follow-up.
Return precautions: numbness, weakness, worsening pain, a cold or pale hand, or recurrent dislocation.
documentation: Anterior shoulder dislocation confirmed; pre-reduction neurovascular exam (including axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function, and the distal pulse) documented.
Any deficit present before reduction recorded as pre-existing, with the time.
Analgesia/sedation method recorded, including intra-articular agent, concentration, and volume if used.
Reduction technique(s) used and number of attempts documented.
Reduction confirmed clinically and on post-reduction imaging.
Post-reduction neurovascular exam documented as intact (or deficits noted, with comparison to the pre-reduction exam).
Immobilization applied and orthopedic follow-up arranged.
seniorPearls: Most failed reductions are failed analgesia. Relax the patient first.
A nerve deficit is not a reason to delay - the nerve is stretched over a displaced humeral head.
Lead with low-force techniques - high-traction methods add fracture and soft-tissue risk.
references: UK Defence Medical Command. Clinical Guidelines for Operations: Joint Dislocations. 2026. https://cgo.mod.uk/clinical-guidelines-for-operations/treatment-guidelines/musculoskeletal/joint-dislocations/
British Elbow and Shoulder Society. Practice guidelines: rehabilitation following traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. 2026. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13056797/

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Shoulder Dislocations - Emergency Department. Updated 2020. https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/fractures/Shoulder_Dislocations_-_Emergency_Department/
Institutional protocols on procedural sedation and intra-articular blocks; verify local practice.

visualAssets.title: Scapular manipulation
visualAssets.subtitle: Scapular manipulation: rotate the scapular tip with slow, steady traction using low force.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Slow, steady force - escalating force abruptly can displace the humeral head further.

shiftMode: Most useful for hip and proximal femur fractures: opioid-sparing analgesia that helps frail and elderly patients.
Confirm no allergy, no infection over the site, and document distal neurovascular function before the block.
Use ultrasound; deposit local anesthetic beneath the fascia iliaca, lateral to the femoral artery and nerve, not into them.
Calculate a weight-based maximum local anesthetic dose and stay under it — these are large-volume blocks.
Aspirate before and during injection to avoid intravascular delivery; watch for LAST.
Confirm spread under the fascia (a lens of fluid lifting the fascia) rather than within muscle.
Have LAST rescue (lipid emulsion) and resuscitation equipment available before you start.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Analgesia for hip fracture (femoral neck, intertrochanteric) and proximal femur fractures
Femoral shaft fracture pain control
Opioid-sparing analgesia in elderly or frail patients where systemic opioids carry higher risk
contraindications: Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Allergy to local anesthetic
Infection or wound over the injection site
Anticoagulation/coagulopathy as a relative risk per local policy
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
anatomy: The fascia iliaca overlies the iliacus and psoas; the femoral nerve runs deep to it.
Target is the compartment beneath the fascia iliaca, lateral to the femoral artery and nerve.
Landmarks: the femoral artery medially and the anterior superior iliac spine laterally; the injection point is lateral to the artery.
Local anesthetic spreads under the fascia to reach the femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with linear (or curvilinear for larger patients) probe and sterile cover
Block needle (e.g., short-bevel or echogenic) and extension tubing
Local anesthetic: 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine, volume from the weight-based calculator on this card. 0.25% ropivacaine is not a supplied strength and is not used here.
Saline for hydrodissection/confirmation
Sterile drape
Aspirating syringe
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel for ultrasound guidance.
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine with the leg slightly externally rotated and the groin exposed.
Place the ultrasound screen in your direct line of sight across the patient.
Clean and drape the area lateral to the femoral pulse.
Identify the femoral artery, nerve, and the fascia iliaca before needling.
steps: Confirm indication, exclude contraindications, and document distal neurovascular function.
Attach monitoring and ensure LAST rescue equipment is immediately available.
Calculate and draw up a weight-based safe dose of local anesthetic.
Prep and drape; scan to identify the femoral artery, femoral nerve, iliacus, and the overlying fascia iliaca.
Choose an entry point lateral to the femoral nerve and artery.
Advance the needle in-plane under ultrasound toward the plane beneath the fascia iliaca.
Confirm tip position with a small test injection that lifts the fascia (hydrodissection), not muscle.
Aspirate, then inject incrementally with repeated aspiration, watching spread under the fascia.
Observe spread tracking medially and laterally beneath the fascia.
Monitor for LAST and reassess analgesia and distal neurovascular status after the block.
ultrasound: Identify the femoral artery and nerve; the fascia iliaca is the hyperechoic layer over iliacus.
Use in-plane needling lateral to the nerve to keep the needle tip in view throughout.
A correct injection lifts the fascia off the muscle as an expanding hypoechoic lens.
If fluid pools within muscle or around the nerve without subfascial spread, reposition before injecting more.
confirmation: Local anesthetic seen spreading beneath the fascia iliaca on ultrasound
No intravascular or intraneural injection (negative aspiration, no spread within the nerve)
Total dose remained below the weight-based maximum
Progressive analgesia in the femoral distribution over the expected onset time
No signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Fluid spreading in muscle, not under the fascia: reposition the tip to the correct plane before continuing.
Blood on aspiration: withdraw and reposition; never inject against a positive aspirate.
Early LAST signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, dysrhythmia): stop injection and begin lipid-emulsion rescue.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor for delayed LAST and reassess analgesia after the expected onset.
Document the block, dose, and post-block neurovascular exam.
Communicate the block to the orthopedic and inpatient teams so a femoral deficit is not misattributed.
Continue multimodal analgesia and reassess pain regularly.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Fascia iliaca compartment block performed for [hip/femur] fracture analgesia.
Contraindications excluded.
Ultrasound-guided subfascial spread confirmed; aspiration negative for blood.
No signs of LAST during or after the procedure.
Post-block analgesia; block communicated to the admitting team.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
seniorPearls: Useful in elderly hip fractures: spares the opioids that drive their delirium and respiratory trouble.
Fluid in muscle rather than under the fascia means no block and a wasted dose near the maximum.
Calculate the maximum dose every time and keep lipid emulsion in the room; large-volume blocks are where LAST happens.

visualAssets.title: Fascia iliaca plane on ultrasound
visualAssets.subtitle: Linear probe placed at the inguinal crease. Identify the femoral artery, fascia lata (superficial), and fascia iliaca (deep). Target the plane deep to fascia iliaca, lateral to the femoral nerve.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Inject lateral to the nerve. Watch for fascial pop and subfascial spread.

visualAssets.title: Inguinal fascial layers
visualAssets.subtitle: From superficial to deep: skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia lata, sartorius/iliopsoas, fascia iliaca, then the femoral nerve and iliacus muscle. The block targets the plane between fascia iliaca and iliacus.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Intravascular injection risk near femoral vessels. Aspirate before injecting.

agents.note: Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. Lower risk of severe cardiotoxicity than bupivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting - do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: This is a last-resort, time-critical trauma procedure.

Signs of life means any one of: a palpable pulse, a measurable blood pressure, spontaneous respiratory effort, pupillary reaction, spontaneous or purposeful movement, or organized cardiac electrical activity. None of the six at any point since injury: do not open.
CPR-duration windows (WTA 2024): under 15 minutes for penetrating trauma, under 10 minutes for blunt. Blunt arrest without signs of life is not an indication at any duration.
Requires an operating theater, a surgeon, and blood — do not open without a surgical destination.
Goals, in order: release tamponade, control intrathoracic hemorrhage, allow internal cardiac massage, and cross-clamp the descending aorta if subdiaphragmatic bleeding is the problem.
Left anterolateral thoracotomy at the 4th/5th intercostal space; extend across the sternum (clamshell) for right-sided or wider access.
Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve to relieve tamponade.
Massive transfusion, surgical backup, and a named destination activated before the incision, not after it.
indications: Penetrating thoracic trauma with signs of life at some point after injury and CPR under 15 minutes - the strongest indication
Penetrating extrathoracic trauma within the same window: consider, but the yield is lower and the source may be abdominal
Blunt trauma arrest with signs of life and CPR under 10 minutes
Traumatic arrest with pericardial tamponade identified on ultrasound and a correctable source
Exsanguinating intrathoracic hemorrhage where an aortic cross-clamp is a bridge to the operating theater
Exsanguinating abdominopelvic hemorrhage is a different branch: laparotomy, or Zone 1 REBOA where it is available and part of the local pathway - not thoracotomy
contraindications: Blunt trauma arrest with no signs of life. Survival is effectively zero and this is not indicated at any CPR duration.
No signs of life at any point since injury, for any mechanism
CPR beyond 15 minutes for penetrating or 10 minutes for blunt trauma
No operating theater, surgeon, or blood available
Injuries clearly incompatible with survival, including devastating head injury
Adult criteria only. Use the pediatric trauma pathway for children.
anatomy: Left anterolateral approach at the 4th-5th intercostal space follows the rib's superior margin to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
The pericardium is opened longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve, which runs along its lateral surface.

The descending thoracic aorta lies posteriorly against the spine. The esophagus lies immediately anterior to it and is the structure most often clamped by mistake - an orogastric tube makes it identifiable by feel.
Clamshell extension across the sternum exposes both pleural cavities and the heart for wider access.
Crossing the sternum divides both internal mammary arteries. They will not bleed while there is no circulation and will bleed hard the moment there is one - find and ligate them.
equipment: Thoracotomy/clamshell tray: scalpel, Mayo scissors, rib spreader (Finochietto retractor)
Sternal-division instrument: heavy trauma shears, a Lebsche knife, or a Gigli saw. Confirm which one is in your tray in advance.
Vascular clamps (aortic and DeBakey-type) for cross-clamping and vessel control
Toothed forceps and large hemostats
Internal defibrillator paddles, and confirmation that they connect to your department's defibrillator - paddle and connector generations are not interchangeable
Suction and large volumes of gauze/laparotomy pads
Massive transfusion products and rapid infuser
Orogastric tube, to identify the esophagus before clamping the aorta
Foley catheter or sutures for temporary cardiac wound control, and a skin stapler for rapid closure
Sterile gloves, gowns, eye protection, and face shields for the whole team
positioning: Patient supine with the left arm raised or abducted to expose the lateral chest.
Operate from the patient's left side for a left anterolateral thoracotomy.
Ensure continued airway management and ongoing resuscitation by the team.
Prep quickly.
steps: Confirm the criteria in shiftMode by the numbers, then activate trauma surgery, massive transfusion, and the theater.
Make a left anterolateral incision at the 4th-5th intercostal space along the superior rib margin, from the sternal edge to the table.
Divide intercostal muscles and enter the pleura; place and open the rib spreader with its handle toward the axilla so it does not sit in the field.
Extend across the sternum (clamshell) if there is right-sided injury or you need wider exposure, then find and ligate both internal mammary arteries.
Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve, and evacuate clot to relieve tamponade. A tamponaded pericardium is tense and hard to pinch up - grasp and incise it.
Control cardiac wounds with finger pressure first, then a Foley balloon, staples, or sutures. Do not tie a suture around a coronary artery.

Internal cardiac massage two-handed. Internal defibrillation only if the rhythm is shockable, and at the low energy internal paddles use - commonly of the order of 10-20 J, confirmed against your paddle and defibrillator instructions.

Cross-clamp the descending aorta only if the bleeding is subdiaphragmatic or you need to redirect what circulation there is to heart and brain. Retract the left lung anteriorly, open the posterior pleura, identify the aorta against the spine with the esophagus anterior to it, and clamp under direct vision.
Say the clamp time out loud when you apply it and every five minutes after. Everything below the clamp is ischemic, and its release is a second resuscitation.
Control intrathoracic bleeding and continue resuscitation with blood products.
Endpoint: no organized cardiac activity after tamponade release, hemorrhage control, and an aortic clamp. Stop there.
Transport immediately to the operating room for definitive repair if circulation is restored.
ultrasound: Ultrasound before or around the arrest can identify tamponade and support the decision to proceed.

Cardiac standstill is not a free-standing reason to stop. In a patient in PEA with no signs of life, absent wall motion on a technically adequate view supports termination. In a patient with signs of life it changes nothing.
Never delay a clearly indicated thoracotomy to get a scan, and never repeat a scan to postpone the decision.
confirmation: Pericardium opened and tamponade relieved if present
Cardiac or great-vessel bleeding controlled
Aorta clamped under direct vision with the esophagus identified, clamp time recorded, and central perfusion improved
Return of organized cardiac activity or perfusing rhythm as the resuscitation endpoint
Patient moving to definitive operative care without delay
troubleshooting: Cannot get exposure: the incision is too short or too high. Extend it to the table and across the sternum.
Cannot find a cardiac wound after opening the pericardium: inspect the posterior surface and great vessels; lift the heart carefully.
Ongoing massive hemorrhage from the chest: pack, control the source, and cross-clamp the aorta while transfusing.
Sudden brisk bleeding after return of circulation in a clamshell: the internal mammary arteries. Look at the sternal edges first.
Clamp is on and nothing changed after a few minutes: question the clamp before the patient. It is probably on the esophagus - check by feel against the orogastric tube - or the bleeding is above it.
Phrenic nerve in the way of pericardiotomy: open anterior to it to avoid injury.
Right-sided injury inaccessible from the left: extend to a clamshell for bilateral exposure.
No response after pericardial release and aortic clamp: reassess for non-survivable injury and the resuscitation endpoint.
complications: Iatrogenic injury to the heart, lung, phrenic nerve, or great vessels
Esophageal injury from clamping the wrong posterior structure
Internal mammary bleeding after clamshell, unmasked by return of circulation
Coronary or aortic injury during clamping
Distal ischemia below the clamp, and the reperfusion physiology when it comes off
Inadequate exposure leading to missed injury
Team blood-borne exposure during a rapid open procedure
Very high mortality given the underlying physiology
aftercare: Move immediately to the operating room for definitive repair if circulation returns.
Release the aortic clamp as early as the patient tolerates, and announce it. Reperfusion drops the pressure and returns the products of ischemia to the circulation.
Hand the clamp on and off times to the surgical team explicitly.
Continue massive transfusion and correct coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.
Debrief the team and address occupational exposures after the resuscitation.
documentation: Resuscitative thoracotomy for [penetrating/blunt] trauma arrest meeting local criteria.
Mechanism, CPR duration in minutes, and which signs of life were present and when, named individually.
Procedure: thoracotomy with or without clamshell, pericardiotomy, hemorrhage control, aortic cross-clamp as applicable.
Aortic clamp application and release times.
Intraoperative findings and interventions.
Resuscitation endpoint and disposition (OR vs. termination) against the criteria used.
Team exposures and debrief.
seniorPearls: Apply the criteria before opening; speed does not rescue a case that never met them.
Open the pericardium anterior to the phrenic nerve and longitudinally; tamponade release is often the single highest-yield action.
The commonest technical failure is a small incision. Cut from the sternum to the table.
If you clamped and nothing changed, question the clamp before you question the patient.
Nothing done here is definitive; the patient goes to theater the moment there is circulation.

Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma. Emergency Department Thoracotomy: Practice Management Guideline. 2015. https://www.east.org/education-resources/practice-management-guidelines/details/emergency-department-thoracotomy

visualAssets.title: Pericardiotomy & phrenic nerve
visualAssets.subtitle: Anterolateral incision, entry at the rib margin, and a longitudinal pericardial opening anterior to the phrenic nerve.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve.

shiftMode: Transition to definitive IV access once stable.
Tibia is the default site when unsure. Humerus flows faster and reaches central circulation sooner in arrest, but is mis-sited more often and dislodges during CPR.
In a responsive patient: lidocaine first, then flush — flushing unanesthetized marrow is painful and wastes the lidocaine.
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free: 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg ceiling. Use the calculator — a flat adult dose can be many times the correct dose for an infant.
Nearly all IV medications and fluids can be given IO. Pressure bag or push-pull syringe for rapid infusion.
Aim to remove within 24 hours. Document site, time in, and reason for IO.
indications: Failed or impossible peripheral IV access in emergent setting
Cardiac arrest when IV access has failed or is not feasible - current adult guidance attempts IV first
Critically ill or injured patient requiring immediate vascular access
Pediatric resuscitation when IV access not rapidly obtained
Severe dehydration with vascular collapse
contraindications: Fracture in the target bone
Attempted or established IO access in the target bone within the past 48 hours
Overlying infection or burn at insertion site
Prosthetic joint or hardware at target site
Conditions with fragile bone (relative: osteogenesis imperfecta, severe osteoporosis)
Excessive tissue over the site, or landmarks that cannot be identified
anatomy: Proximal tibia: flat anteromedial surface, 1-2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity.
Proximal humerus: greater tubercle, arm adducted and internally rotated with the hand on the abdomen. Insert at 45 degrees to the anterior plane aimed posteromedially - not 90 degrees.
Distal tibia: medial malleolus, 1-2 cm proximal to the most prominent point.
In pediatrics the proximal tibia is preferred; the flat medial tibial surface is more accessible.
equipment: EZ-IO driver with needle sets: 15 mm (3-39 kg), 25 mm (40 kg and above), 45 mm (excess tissue, and the proximal humerus in most adults)
Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
Gloves, eye protection
Normal saline flush syringes sized to the patient: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free, for responsive patients
Extension tubing and IV setup
Pressure bag for fluid infusion
Stabilizer/dressing to secure IO needle
Sharps container
positioning: Proximal tibia: leg slightly externally rotated, small towel roll behind the knee.
Proximal humerus: arm adducted, hand on abdomen to internally rotate.
Stabilize the limb. Do not place your hand behind the insertion point.
steps: Identify the insertion site and confirm no contraindications at that limb.
Clean the site with antiseptic.
Stabilize the limb without placing your hand behind the target bone.
Select the needle by tissue depth rather than age: 15 mm for 3-39 kg, 25 mm for 40 kg and above, 45 mm for excess tissue and for the proximal humerus in most adults.
Attach the needle to the driver and touch the tip to bone. At least the 5 mm mark must be visible above the skin before you drill; if it is not, change to a longer needle.
Trajectory is site-specific: 90 degrees to bone at the tibia and distal femur; 45 degrees to the anterior plane, aimed posteromedially, at the proximal humerus.
Drill until loss of resistance (a subtle give or pop).
Remove the trocar, attach a syringe, and aspirate (marrow aspirate confirms placement but is not always obtained).

In a responsive patient give preservative-free, epinephrine-free lidocaine 2% at the weight-based dose on the max-dose card, slowly over about 120 seconds. Do not flush first - the marrow distension caused by the flush is the pain the lidocaine exists to prevent.
Allow about 60 seconds of dwell, then flush: 5-10 mL normal saline in adults, 2-5 mL in infants and children.
Connect IV tubing with extension set. Use pressure bag for rapid infusion.
Secure the needle and apply stabilizer dressing.
Document time of insertion, site, confirmation method, and complications.
confirmation: Needle stands upright without support after insertion
Loss of resistance felt during drilling
Marrow aspirate on syringe (not always present; absence does not rule out placement)
Saline flush flows freely without subcutaneous swelling
Medications and fluids infuse without extravasation
troubleshooting: No flow after insertion: ensure trocar removed, recheck position, attempt gentle flush. If extravasation seen, remove and attempt different bone.
Needle loose or wobbly: likely through-and-through cortex penetration. Remove and use a different site.

Significant pain in a responsive patient: give the weight-based lidocaine dose over 120 seconds and allow the 60-second dwell before flushing. About half the initial dose can be repeated if pain recurs.
Swelling at site: extravasation indicates malposition. Remove needle, compress, reassess compartment.
Lidocaine given but no effect in a small child: check the extension set. At pediatric volumes the set's dead space can hold most of the dose - prime it, or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
complications: Osteomyelitis (rare, risk increases if left in >24 hours)
Fracture (rare, more common with manual devices in pediatrics)
Pain during infusion in conscious patients
aftercare: Transition to peripheral or central IV access as soon as feasible.

Aim to remove the IO within 24 hours. Labelling permits up to 48 hours in selected patients aged 12 and over when no alternative access exists - do not pull a patient's only access to meet a deadline.
Document insertion time, site, removal time, and any complications.
Monitor insertion site for signs of infection, swelling, or compartment syndrome.
documentation: IO access at [site] using [device] for [indication].
Verbal/implied consent in emergent setting.
Site prepped, needle inserted with loss of resistance confirmed.
Flushed with [volume] normal saline without extravasation.
IO lidocaine before infusion (if conscious).
Procedure tolerated; removal within 24 hours and transition to definitive access.
seniorPearls: IO is not a last resort. If you cannot get a peripheral line in a crashing patient in 90 seconds, drill.
The proximal humerus flows faster than the tibia in adults. Know both sites.
Lidocaine before the flush, not after. Three minutes including the dwell.
Through-and-through is a real risk in peds. Use the correct needle length and stop at loss of resistance.
The 5 mm mark beats any weight chart: it measures how much needle is left after the tissue.
references: Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO intraosseous vascular access procedure template, document MCI-2019-0395. https://www.teleflex.com/global/clinical-resources/documents/MCI-2019-0395_Arrow_EZ-IO_Intraosseous_Procedure_Template_LR.pdf

Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO procedure competency template, MC-000270 rev 2c. 2021. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/clinical-resources/ez-io/documents/EM_IOS_EZIO%20Procedure-Competency-Template_MC-000270_rev2c.pdf
Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO indications and contraindications data sheet. https://go.teleflex.com/EZUI-Procedure-Tray-Data-Sheet.html

American Heart Association. 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC: Adult Advanced Life Support, vascular access. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

visualAssets.title: Proximal tibia insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Palpate the tibial tuberosity. Move 1-2 cm distal and medial to the flat anteromedial tibial surface. This is the insertion point. Needle at 90 degrees to the bone.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Do not place your hand behind the limb during drilling.

visualAssets.title: Proximal humerus insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Arm adducted, hand on abdomen (internal rotation). Palpate the greater tubercle — the most prominent lateral bony point of the shoulder. Needle at 90 degrees to the bone surface.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Humeral IO flows faster than tibial in adults. Secure well — humeral IOs dislodge more easily.

agents.note: Preservative-free and epinephrine-free only. Adults are given 40 mg initially regardless of weight; infants and children get 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg maximum, which is the figure computed here.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
caveats: This is the dose to give, not a range to stay under.
At pediatric volumes the extension set's dead space can hold most of the dose. Prime the set or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
monitoring: Infuse slowly over about 120 seconds, then allow a 60-second dwell before flushing.
Flush volume is age-specific: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child.
Reassess the site and the whole limb for extravasation before every infusion.

shiftMode: Superolateral approach is the most common. Medial approach is an alternative.
Always send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Use sterile technique - the tap itself can seed a septic joint.
Tap before antibiotics if the patient can wait a few minutes. If septic or in shock: antibiotics first (blood cultures first), tap after — document the sample as post-antibiotic.
Ultrasound guidance increases success, especially in obese patients or small effusions.
Document appearance of fluid: clear, turbid, bloody, purulent.
indications: Acute monoarticular arthritis to evaluate for septic joint
Crystal arthropathy workup (gout, pseudogout)
Hemarthrosis evaluation
Symptomatic relief of tense effusion
Traumatic effusion with concern for intra-articular fracture or lipohemarthrosis
contraindications: Overlying cellulitis or skin infection at planned insertion site
Significant coagulopathy (relative; weigh risk vs. benefit if septic joint is suspected)
Prosthetic joint (consult orthopedics before tapping)
Patient refusal
anatomy: Superolateral approach: needle enters 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superolateral pole of the patella, directed toward the intercondylar notch.
Medial approach: needle enters at the midpoint of the patella on the medial side, directed posterolaterally.
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint and is an alternative US-guided target.
Avoid the popliteal fossa (posterior neurovascular structures).
equipment: Sterile gloves and drape
Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
Local anesthetic: 5 mL of 1% lidocaine, with a 25G needle for the skin wheal
18G needle and 20-60 mL syringe for aspiration

Sterile containers for the primary samples, with the remaining fluid inoculated into blood culture bottles. Confirm tube colors and whether the laboratory accepts a culture bottle as the primary specimen with the lab that will run it.
Sterile dressing
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe (if available)
Hemostat (optional, for syringe exchange)
positioning: Patient supine with knee in slight flexion (15-20 degrees). A rolled towel behind the knee helps.
Relaxed quadriceps. The patella should be mobile.
Identify landmarks or use ultrasound to confirm effusion location.
steps: Confirm indication and obtain consent.
Position the knee in slight flexion. Identify landmarks or use ultrasound.
Prep the insertion site with antiseptic using sterile technique.
Anesthetize the skin and subcutaneous tissue with lidocaine down to the capsule.
Insert the 18G needle at the chosen approach, advancing toward the joint space while applying gentle negative pressure on the syringe.
Aspirate fluid. If using a large syringe, a hemostat can stabilize the needle during syringe exchange.
Remove as much fluid as clinically appropriate for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
Remove the needle and apply sterile dressing.
Send fluid for cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Document volume, appearance, and studies sent.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe placed over the suprapatellar recess (longitudinal) to confirm effusion.
Anechoic fluid collection confirms effusion. Complex or echogenic fluid may suggest infection or hemorrhage.
Use in-plane needle guidance for real-time visualization.
Particularly useful in obese patients or when clinical exam is equivocal.
confirmation: Synovial fluid aspirated into syringe
Knee effusion clinically reduced after aspiration
Fluid sent for appropriate laboratory studies
troubleshooting: Dry tap: reposition needle, use ultrasound guidance, consider smaller effusion or loculated collection.
Bloody aspirate: may be hemarthrosis or traumatic tap. Send for analysis. Lipohemarthrosis on gross inspection suggests intra-articular fracture.
Difficulty advancing needle: may be hitting bone. Redirect slightly.
Patient unable to relax quadriceps: coach relaxation, ensure adequate local anesthesia.
complications: Iatrogenic septic arthritis (rare with proper sterile technique)
aftercare: Instruct patient on signs of infection: increasing pain, redness, warmth, fever.
Keep dressing clean and dry for 24 hours.
Follow up on culture and crystal results.

If septic arthritis is suspected, treat and admit rather than waiting for a number. Sepsis or septic shock: empiric antibiotics immediately, before or without the aspirate. Tap first only when the patient can safely wait for it.
documentation: Knee arthrocentesis performed on [side] knee for [indication].
Informed consent obtained.
Site prepped with sterile technique. Local anesthesia administered.
Aspirated [volume] mL of [appearance] fluid using [approach].
Fluid sent for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Patient tolerated procedure without immediate complication.
Sterile dressing applied.
seniorPearls: If you are debating whether to tap a hot swollen joint, tap it.
Ultrasound turns a blind procedure into a guided one.
Clear straw-colored fluid at the bedside does not rule out infection. Send the labs.

No synovial white cell count rules septic arthritis in or out. Above 50,000 raises the probability without confirming it; below 50,000 does not exclude it, particularly early, in the immunocompromised, and in prosthetic joints. Crystals do not exclude infection - gout and a septic joint can coexist in the same knee.
references: European Bone and Joint Infection Society. Guideline for the management of septic arthritis in native joints (SANJO). J Bone Jt Infect. 2023;8(1):29-37. https://doi.org/10.5194/jbji-8-29-2023
