caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Most anterior epistaxis is from Kiesselbach plexus on the septum.
Start with direct pressure: pinch the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes continuously.
If a single bleeding point is visible, silver nitrate cautery may stop the bleed without packing.
If packing is needed, Rapid Rhino or Merocel sponge are first-line devices.
Always check vitals and hemodynamic stability. Posterior bleeds and anticoagulated patients can hemorrhage.
Patients discharged with packing need ENT follow-up for removal in 48-72 hours.
indications: Anterior epistaxis uncontrolled by direct pressure
Visible anterior bleeding source amenable to packing
Recurrent epistaxis requiring temporizing control
Post-cautery reinforcement when bleeding recurs
contraindications: Suspected posterior epistaxis (pack both if unavoidable, but involve ENT early)
Suspected nasal fracture with CSF leak
Severe midface trauma requiring operative management
anatomy: Kiesselbach plexus: anterior septum, the most common source of anterior epistaxis.
Supplied by branches of anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and greater palatine arteries.
The nasal cavity narrows posteriorly. Packing must fill the anterior space to tamponade the vessel.
Direct packing along the nasal floor, not upward toward the cribriform plate.
equipment: Personal protective equipment (gown, gloves, face shield)
Headlamp or bright light source
Nasal speculum
Suction with Frazier tip
Topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline spray or phenylephrine-soaked pledgets)

Topical anesthetic: 4% lidocaine on cotton pledgets - 40 mg per milliliter. Nasal mucosa absorbs close to intravenous rates; 2-3 mL is 80-120 mg. It counts against the same ceiling as injected local anesthetic, so do not keep re-soaking pledgets to hold the field.
Silver nitrate sticks (for cautery if appropriate)
Nasal packing device: Rapid Rhino, Merocel sponge, or ribbon gauze with petroleum jelly
Resorbable packing for patients with a bleeding disorder or on antithrombotic therapy.
Sterile water to activate a Rapid Rhino's hydrocolloid coating, and a separate syringe of air for its cuff. Water outside the pack, air inside; saline goes in neither.
Antibiotic ointment (for gauze packing)
Kidney basin and gauze for blood management
1g Tranexamic acid (TXA) for topical use; injectable solution applied on a pledget or used to soak the pack
positioning: Patient seated upright leaning slightly forward to prevent blood swallowing.
Have the patient blow out clots gently before examination.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets for 10-15 minutes before instrumentation.
steps: Ensure hemodynamic stability. Obtain IV access if significant bleeding or anticoagulation.
Apply PPE.
Have the patient blow out clots. Suction the nasal cavity.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets. Wait 10-15 minutes.
Remove pledgets and inspect with nasal speculum and headlamp to identify bleeding source.
If a single anterior point is identified and bleeding is controlled: apply silver nitrate to the site for 5-10 seconds. Do not cauterize both sides of the septum simultaneously (perforation risk).
If cautery fails or bleeding is diffuse: proceed to nasal packing.

Rapid Rhino: soak the pack in sterile water for at least 30 seconds to activate the hydrocolloid coating, insert along the nasal floor, then inflate the cuff slowly with air only, using the pilot cuff to judge it. Saline or water in the cuff is contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
Merocel sponge: insert dry sponge along the nasal floor, then hydrate with saline to expand.
Confirm hemostasis. Check for posterior drainage in the oropharynx.
If bilateral packing is placed, monitor for hypoxia in high-risk patients.
confirmation: Active bleeding has stopped
No posterior drainage seen in the oropharynx on inspection
Packing is seated properly and not extruding
Patient hemodynamically stable
troubleshooting: Continued bleeding after packing: ensure packing fills the anterior cavity adequately. May need additional packing or posterior epistaxis management.
Posterior bleed suspected: blood draining in posterior pharynx despite adequate anterior packing. Place posterior balloon or consult ENT urgently.

Patient on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet: local measures first - pressure, vasoconstrictor, cautery, resorbable packing. Reserve reversal or withholding the drug for life-threatening bleeding, and refer that decision to the prescribing team or hematology, jointly with ENT.
Vasovagal during packing: recline patient, maintain airway, resume when stable.
complications: Nasal septal necrosis or pressure injury (if packing too tight or left too long)
Sinusitis or toxic shock syndrome (rare, from prolonged packing)
aftercare: Discharge with packing in place. Arrange ENT follow-up for removal in 48-72 hours.
Antibiotics after packing are not automatic. Toxic shock syndrome after nasal packing is rare, and routine prophylaxis has not been shown to prevent it.
Instruct patient to keep head elevated, avoid straining, nose blowing, and blood thinners if safe to hold.
Return precautions: recurrent heavy bleeding, difficulty breathing, fever, significant swelling.
documentation: Anterior epistaxis managed with [method: cautery / packing device].
Bleeding source identified on [side] anterior septum.
Bleeding-risk factors recorded: anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy with the agent and last dose, known bleeding disorder, liver disease, hypertension.
Topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic applied, with the agent, concentration, and approximate amount.
[Cautery performed / packing placed]: device, side, whether resorbable, and inflation medium if applicable.
Removal plan documented with the date and who will remove it.
No posterior drainage observed.
Patient hemodynamically stable. Discharged with ENT follow-up arranged and the transition of care recorded.
Return precautions given.
seniorPearls: Fifteen minutes of real continuous pressure stops most anterior bleeds.
Suction, vasoconstrict, and light the field before touching anything.
Do not cauterize both sides of the septum.
Check the oropharynx - a posterior bleed masquerades as anterior packing failure.
references: Tunkel DE, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(1_suppl):S1-S38. https://doi.org/10.1177/0194599819890327
Smith+Nephew. RAPID RHINO usage instructions. https://rapidrhino.com/usage-instructions/

AAO-HNSF. Nosebleed guideline research needs. 2020. https://www.entnet.org/resource/cpg-nosebleed-epistaxis-research-needs/ - The benefit and the ideal duration of antibiotic prophylaxis after nasal packing are both identified as unresolved research questions.

Zahed R, et al. A new and rapid method for epistaxis treatment using injectable form of tranexamic acid topically: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Emerg Med. 2013;31(9):1389-1392. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajem.2013.06.043
Verify institutional policy on antibiotic prophylaxis with nasal packing, and read the instructions for use of the specific pack your department stocks.

agents.note: Applied topically on pledgets here, not injected. Nasal mucosa absorbs close to intravenous rates, so it counts against this same ceiling in full.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before soaking the first pledget - say it out loud.
Count every pledget against the running total; re-soaking a pledget is a second dose, not a top-up.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Confirm SYNC mode is on before shocking — it times the shock to the R wave.
Unstable = cardiovert now. Stable = consider rate control, rhythm control, or elective cardioversion.
Signs of instability: hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure.
Sedate before cardioversion unless peri-arrest — doses, monitoring, and rescue are on the procedural sedation card.
If the patient deteriorates into pulseless VT or VF, switch to defibrillation (SYNC off, max energy).
Initial biphasic energy: atrial fibrillation 200 J, atrial flutter 200 J, narrow-complex SVT 100 J, monomorphic VT with a pulse 100 J.
Manufacturer's recommended energy takes precedence over the figures above — find out what your machine says before the night you need it.
Escalate toward the device maximum if a shock fails rather than repeating the same energy.
indications: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse (SVT, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, monomorphic VT with a pulse)
Elective cardioversion of persistent atrial fibrillation or flutter, once the anticoagulation or imaging pathway below is satisfied
Wide complex tachycardia with hemodynamic compromise
contraindications: Pulseless VT or VF (requires unsynchronized defibrillation, not cardioversion)
Polymorphic VT (unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy; the device cannot synchronize to it)
Known left atrial or left atrial appendage thrombus - an absolute contraindication to elective cardioversion

Elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation lasting 48 hours or longer, or of unknown duration, without either three weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or transesophageal echo excluding thrombus
Digitalis toxicity-related arrhythmia (relative; cardioversion may precipitate refractory VF)
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (will not respond; treat underlying cause)
Sinus tachycardia (not an indication for cardioversion; treat the cause)
anatomy: Anterolateral pad placement: right parasternal and left lateral chest wall (V5-V6 position at the mid-axillary line).
Anteroposterior placement: sternum and left infrascapular area. May be superior for atrial fibrillation.

Do not place a pad over an implanted device generator. Keep at least 8 cm away, prefer anteroposterior, and confirm the separation your device and defibrillator manufacturers state rather than treating 8 cm as universal.
Any pacemaker or ICD needs interrogation after cardioversion. A shock can alter programming or damage the device.
Remove transdermal medication patches from the pad path. A metal-backed patch can arc and burn.
equipment: Defibrillator/cardioverter with SYNC capability, and knowledge of its recommended energies and its SYNC-persistence behavior
Adhesive defibrillation pads (preferred over paddles)
Continuous cardiac monitor with 12-lead ECG capability
Sedation per the procedural sedation card - agents, doses, monitoring, and rescue requirements
Airway equipment including bag-valve mask, oral airway, suction, and intubation supplies at bedside
Pulse oximetry and continuous waveform capnography
IV access (ideally two sites)
Resuscitation medications (epinephrine, amiodarone, atropine) at bedside
Crash cart
positioning: Patient supine. Pads placed with good skin contact (shave excess chest hair if needed, wipe moisture).
Pads pressed down over their whole surface, and not overlapping ECG electrodes or medication patches - both cause burns and both raise impedance.
Clear the area around the patient before shock delivery.
Ensure monitor leads are connected and rhythm is visible.
steps: Confirm the indication: identify the rhythm, confirm hemodynamic instability or elective plan.
Obtain 12-lead ECG if time permits.
Establish IV access. Place monitoring (pulse ox, capnography, cardiac monitor).
Prepare airway equipment at bedside.
Apply defibrillation pads in anterolateral or anteroposterior position.
Administer procedural sedation per that card if the patient is conscious and not peri-arrest. Confirm depth before charging.
Select the energy for the rhythm, cross-checked against your defibrillator's recommended dose. Activate SYNC mode.
Verify SYNC markers are tracking R waves on the monitor.
Announce "Charging" and charge the defibrillator.
Perform a visual and verbal safety check: "I am clear, you are clear, everyone is clear."
Deliver the shock. Hold the shock button until the device fires (SYNC mode may have a brief delay).

Assess the rhythm immediately. If unsuccessful, escalate the energy rather than repeating the same one. Confirm SYNC on the screen before every shock - whether a device holds SYNC or drops it after a shock is configurable on current Philips and LIFEPAK platforms.
If the patient becomes pulseless, immediately switch to defibrillation protocol.
confirmation: Post-shock rhythm is converted to sinus or target rhythm
Hemodynamic improvement (blood pressure, mentation, perfusion)
Repeat 12-lead ECG shows new rhythm
troubleshooting: Shock does not fire: SYNC mode waits for an R wave. If the rhythm is too irregular or amplitude is too low, the device may not fire. Try a different lead, increase ECG gain, or switch to unsynchronized defibrillation if the patient is deteriorating.
Rhythm unchanged after shock: escalate the energy, ensure good pad contact, try anteroposterior pad position.
Patient moves or remembers the shock: sedation failure. Do not shock a conscious patient again without deepening sedation unless they are peri-arrest.
Patient deteriorates to VF or pulseless VT: immediately switch to unsynchronized defibrillation at max energy.
Post-cardioversion bradycardia: observe, atropine if symptomatic, transcutaneous pacing at bedside.
Recurrence of arrhythmia: consider antiarrhythmic medication before repeating cardioversion.
complications: Skin burns at pad sites, worse with poor contact, chest hair, or a shock delivered over an ECG electrode or medication patch
Thromboembolism (stroke) if atrial fibrillation cardioverted without adequate anticoagulation
Implanted pacemaker or ICD damage or reprogramming
aftercare: Monitor until the rhythm is stable and the sedation has resolved against the discharge criteria on the procedural sedation card. There is no evidence-based universal telemetry duration for cardioversion itself - the observation period is a local policy decision driven by the arrhythmia, the sedation, and comorbidity.
Repeat 12-lead ECG.
Assess for chest wall discomfort and skin burns at pad sites.
Interrogate any pacemaker or ICD.

Anticoagulation after cardioversion: at least four weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation for anyone cardioverted from atrial fibrillation or flutter, whatever the pre-procedure duration, and then long-term by stroke risk rather than by whether the rhythm held.
An unstable patient cardioverted without the pre-procedure pathway still needs the post-procedure anticoagulation.
documentation: Synchronized cardioversion for [rhythm] with [indication].
Pre-procedure rhythm on 12-lead ECG.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter: duration, and which pre-procedure pathway applied - anticoagulation, imaging, or urgent without either.
Sedation: [agent, dose, route]. Adequate depth achieved.
SYNC mode confirmed. [Energy] J via biphasic defibrillator, with the device model recorded.
Post-shock rhythm: [rhythm]. Hemodynamics [stable/improved].
Patient tolerated procedure without immediate complication.
Post-procedure 12-lead ECG. Monitoring, device interrogation, and anticoagulation plan.
seniorPearls: Look at SYNC on the screen before every shock. Whether a device holds it or drops it depends on the model and its configuration.
The shock button delay in SYNC mode confuses people. Hold the button until it fires.
The first shock is the one most likely to work. Do not spend it on a low energy chosen out of caution.
Anteroposterior pad placement is better for atrial fibrillation. If anterolateral fails, switch before escalating energy.
Do not cardiovert sinus tachycardia. Find and fix the cause.
If the rhythm is polymorphic VT, treat it as VF: unsynchronized defibrillation, not synchronized cardioversion.
Interrogate the pacemaker afterwards.
references: American Heart Association. Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. 2025. https://www.heart.org/-/media/CPR-Files/CPR-Guidelines-Files/2025-Algorithms/Algorithm-ACLS-Electrical-Cardioversion-250514.pdf

American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines - synchronized cardioversion energy and manufacturer dose deference. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support — AHA states at least 200 J is reasonable for fibrillation and that 200 J may be reasonable for flutter (a stronger recommendation for fibrillation than flutter), replacing the older practice of starting low and climbing since a failed low-energy shock costs the patient another sedation and another shock; AHA also defers to the manufacturer's stated dose, as biphasic waveforms are not interchangeable across devices.
Joglar JA, et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation. 2024;149(1):e1-e156. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Read your defibrillator's operating instructions for its recommended cardioversion energies, SYNC-persistence configuration, and implanted-device clearance. Philips HeartStart Intrepid and Stryker LIFEPAK 15 are examples: https://www.stryker.com/content/dam/stryker/ems/resources/operating-instructions/international/3314911-030_int-eng_lifepak_15_operating_instructions.pdf
Verify institutional cardioversion and sedation protocols.

shiftMode: Needle aspiration, I&D, and abscess tonsillectomy are all effective — aspiration is the usual bedside choice. Follow local ENT preference where one exists.
Decide first whether this patient can have anything done at the bedside at all. See contraindications - the airway question comes before the technique question.
Limit needle depth to 1 cm with a guard (cut syringe sheath or tape).
Aspirate at the point of maximal fluctuance or bulging, usually the superior pole of the tonsil.
Always have suction ready - these patients aspirate pus.
If you cannot aspirate pus but clinical suspicion is high, consider CT with contrast or ENT consultation.
indications: Clinically suspected peritonsillar abscess (unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice)
Confirmed peritonsillar abscess on imaging or clinical exam
Failed outpatient antibiotic therapy for peritonsillar cellulitis progressing to abscess
contraindications: Any airway warning sign: stridor, drooling or inability to handle secretions, respiratory distress, a tripoding or sniffing posture, or hypoxia. These patients need a controlled airway plan with ENT or anesthesia, not a needle at the bedside.
Severe sepsis or septic shock - resuscitate and involve ENT and critical care; drainage still needs to happen, but not as an unmonitored bedside procedure.
Concern for deep space neck infection extending beyond the peritonsillar space: neck swelling, torticollis, trismus out of proportion, or pain on neck movement. Image and consult ENT or surgery.
Pulsatile mass or bruit suggesting vascular anomaly (get imaging first)
Severe trismus preventing adequate visualization - sedation or operative drainage.
Patient unable to cooperate (relative; consider procedural sedation, and if sedation is needed then the monitoring on the procedural sedation card applies)
Bedside drainage requires suction, oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment immediately to hand. Without them, move to a room that has them.
anatomy: The peritonsillar space lies between the tonsillar capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle.
The internal carotid artery runs posterolateral, typically 2-2.5 cm from the pharyngeal mucosal surface.
Most PTAs collect at the superior pole of the tonsil, between the anterior tonsillar pillar and the soft palate.
Uvular deviation is typically away from the affected side.
The palatine tonsil, anterior and posterior pillars, and soft palate are key landmarks.
equipment: Headlamp or good overhead light
Tongue depressor

Topical anesthetic spray. With a benzocaine product such as Cetacaine, keep to the shortest labelled spray - about one second - and do not repeat it: benzocaine sprays carry an FDA warning for methemoglobinemia, which can be fatal, and the mouth and pharynx absorb quickly. A lidocaine-based topical is the safer default.
Local anesthetic: lidocaine 1% with epinephrine, 3 mL syringe, 25G needle
Aspiration: 18G needle on a 10 mL syringe
Needle guard: tape or cut syringe cap placed 1 cm from needle tip
Suction with Yankauer tip, tested before you start
Oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment in the room
Kidney basin
Specimen cup for culture
Methylene blue available in the department if benzocaine is used - the treatment for methemoglobinemia; the sign is cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen
positioning: Patient seated upright, leaning slightly forward.
Good light source directed at the oropharynx.
Tongue depressor in the non-dominant hand.
Suction immediately available.
Have the patient open mouth maximally. If trismus limits opening, topical anesthetic and gentle approach or sedation may be needed.
steps: Confirm the diagnosis clinically: unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, muffled voice, trismus.
Apply topical anesthetic spray to the area of planned aspiration.
Inject local anesthetic (1% lidocaine with epinephrine) into the mucosa overlying the abscess. Aspirate first to exclude vascular puncture.
Attach an 18G needle to a 10 mL syringe. Place a needle guard at 1 cm from the tip.
Insert the needle at the point of maximal fluctuance (usually the superior pole, at the junction of the anterior pillar and soft palate).
Aspirate while advancing slowly up to 1 cm only.
If pus is obtained: aspirate as much as possible. Send sample for culture.
If no pus is obtained: redirect the needle slightly inferior or medial. A second attempt at the middle pole may be tried.
If no pus after 2-3 attempts: consider CT to confirm abscess vs. cellulitis, or consult ENT.
After drainage, have the patient gargle and spit. Reassess the oropharynx.
ultrasound: Intraoral ultrasound (endocavitary probe with a cover) can identify the abscess collection and confirm depth.
Transcutaneous submandibular approach may help identify large collections.
Particularly useful when clinical exam is equivocal or prior aspiration was dry.
confirmation: Purulent material aspirated
Improvement in uvular deviation and tonsillar swelling
Patient reports subjective improvement in swallowing and pain
Reduced trismus
troubleshooting: Dry tap: reposition needle to a different quadrant. Consider imaging if repeated attempts fail.
Trismus limiting access: topical anesthetic, consider procedural sedation, or refer to ENT for operative drainage.

Significant bleeding: apply pressure with gauze, maintain suction, most minor mucosal bleeding is self-limited. Pulsatile or brisk bleeding is a different problem - secure the airway and get ENT and vascular help.
Cyanosis or low saturations after a benzocaine spray, not improving with oxygen: methemoglobinemia. Stop the agent, give oxygen, send a co-oximetry level, and treat with methylene blue.
Large abscess with rapid re-accumulation: ENT consultation for incision and drainage or tonsillectomy.
complications: Aspiration of pus into the airway
Injury to the internal carotid artery (prevented by needle depth guard)
Infection spread to deep neck spaces
aftercare: Oral antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin. Follow institutional guidelines for dose and duration.
Pain management: NSAIDs and paracetamol.

Single-dose corticosteroid - dexamethasone is the agent studied - is a reasonable adjunct for pain and trismus. The evidence is limited and heterogeneous and supports one dose, not a multi-day tapering pack.
Confirm the patient can swallow before discharge - watch them drink something.
Encourage oral hydration. Soft diet.
ENT follow-up within 2-3 days for reassessment.
Return precautions: worsening pain, inability to swallow, difficulty breathing, fever, neck swelling.
documentation: Peritonsillar abscess drainage via needle aspiration performed.
Informed consent obtained.
Topical and local anesthesia applied to [side] peritonsillar area.
Needle inserted at superior pole with depth guard at 1 cm.
Aspirated [volume] mL of purulent material. Sent for culture.
Patient tolerated procedure without complication.
Antibiotics prescribed. ENT follow-up arranged. Return precautions discussed.
seniorPearls: If the patient cannot open their mouth, do not force it. Sedate or consult ENT.
Most PTAs are at the superior pole. If your first aspiration is dry, try there before giving up.
These patients look terrible but get dramatically better within minutes of drainage.
The internal carotid lies posterolateral to the tonsil, typically 2-2.5 cm from the mucosal surface; the 1 cm guard is the margin against it.
references: Windfuhr JP, et al. Clinical practice guideline: tonsillitis II. Surgical management. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2016;273(4):989-1009. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00405-016-3904-x — no drainage technique is established as superior; needle aspiration is often preferred at the bedside because it does not require surgical training.

DailyMed. Cetacaine Topical Anesthetic prescribing information, including the methemoglobinemia warning. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=af1773c5-5d5b-4278-b551-30ad2df6d5b5
Chau JKM, et al. Corticosteroids in peritonsillar abscess treatment: a blinded placebo-controlled clinical trial. Laryngoscope. 2014;124(1):97-103. https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.24283
Verify institutional antibiotic guidelines, the topical anaesthetic on your formulary, and ENT referral pathways.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: X-ray finds most glass, metal, gravel, and bone — it's not a rule-out. Small fragments, some glass, and ceramic are missed; a negative film with a persistent story needs ultrasound or CT, not reassurance.
X-ray does not reliably show wood, plastic, or thorns at all. Ultrasound is the bedside tool for those.
Get adequate anesthesia and a bloodless field before starting.
A digital tourniquet must come off — use a device you can't miss, note the time, and check the finger after (see equipment and aftercare).
If you cannot find it in a reasonable time or it is near critical structures, stop and refer.
Document what you found, what you removed, and what imaging showed. If retained FB is possible, tell the patient.
Tetanus status and wound infection risk should be addressed at every visit.
indications: Known or suspected retained foreign body in soft tissue
Wound with mechanism suggesting foreign body (glass, wood, metal)
Non-healing wound or recurrent infection suggesting retained material
Patient-reported foreign body sensation
contraindications: Foreign body near major neurovascular structures requiring operative exploration
Deep foreign body not accessible with bedside techniques
Foreign body that is asymptomatic, deeply embedded, and not causing infection (may be observed in select cases)
Inadequate anesthesia or equipment for safe removal
anatomy: Hand and foot foreign bodies are near tendons, nerves, and vessels in tight compartments.
Plantar foot: flexor tendons, digital nerves, and plantar fascia are at risk during deep exploration.
The depth and tissue plane of the foreign body dictate the approach. Imaging helps plan.
equipment: Local anesthetic: 1% or 2% lidocaine, with epinephrine where the field allows it
Syringe and needle for anesthesia (25-27G)
Antiseptic prep
Sterile gloves and drape
Scalpel (#11 or #15 blade)
Hemostats (mosquito and Kelly)
Fine-tipped forceps (splinter forceps or Adson)
Iris scissors
Needle driver
Wound irrigation supplies (saline, 18G angiocath on 30-60 mL syringe)

Digit tourniquet that cannot be forgotten: a brightly colored commercial ring tourniquet, or a glove finger or Penrose secured with a large clamp left hanging outside the drape. Not a rolled glove finger tucked under a dressing.
A clock or timer, and something to write the application time on - the drape, the notes, or the patient's chart
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe
Suture material for closure if needed
positioning: Position the affected area for optimal access, lighting, and comfort.
Digit procedures: apply the tourniquet only after the field is prepped, record the time of application out loud and in writing, and leave the device visible outside the drape.
Ensure the patient is comfortable and the field is well-lit.
steps: Obtain history: mechanism, timing, material type, symptoms since injury.
Examine the wound. Assess for signs of infection, neurovascular status distally.
Image the area: X-ray for radiopaque materials, ultrasound for radiolucent objects. A negative X-ray with a story that still fits does not close the question.
Mark the foreign body location on the skin using imaging guidance if needed.
Anesthetize the area with local or regional block as appropriate.
Prep and drape the wound.
Digits: apply the tourniquet now, record the time, and leave the device visible.
If the foreign body is visible or superficial: extract with forceps.
If deeper: make a small incision over the marked location. Blunt dissect along tissue planes using hemostats.
Use ultrasound in real-time to guide your approach to deeper or radiolucent foreign bodies.
Grasp and remove the foreign body. Inspect it for fragmentation.
Irrigate the wound with normal saline.
Reassess the wound. Obtain post-removal imaging if fragmentation is suspected.
Remove the tourniquet and say so out loud. Record the removal time and the total tourniquet time.
Confirm the digit is perfused: capillary refill and color, compared with the neighbouring finger.
Close the wound if appropriate (clean, non-infected, within time window). Leave contaminated or infected wounds open.
Apply appropriate dressing - and confirm again that the tourniquet is not under it.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe (10-15 MHz) provides best resolution for superficial foreign bodies.
Foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures, often with posterior shadowing (glass, metal) or reverberation artifact.
Wood may appear as a hyperechoic linear structure with dirty shadowing.
Scan in two orthogonal planes to localize in 3D.
Real-time ultrasound guidance during extraction improves success for deep or small foreign bodies.
confirmation: Foreign body visualized and removed intact
Post-removal imaging shows no retained fragments (if indicated). Negative imaging is not proof of complete removal when the object may be radiolucent or fragmented.
Wound irrigated and inspected
Tourniquet removed, removal time recorded, and the digit confirmed pink with normal capillary refill
Neurovascular status intact after removal
troubleshooting: Cannot locate foreign body: reimage with ultrasound, try a different scanning plane, consider CT for deep or small objects. Ultrasound sensitivity falls with depth, small size, and operator inexperience; a negative scan is not an answer on its own.
Fragmented foreign body: remove what is accessible, image to assess residual, discuss with patient and consider specialist referral.
Significant bleeding during exploration: apply direct pressure, tourniquet for digits, consider specialist referral for deep structures.
Foreign body near nerve or tendon: stop if safe extraction is not possible. Refer to hand surgery or appropriate specialist.
Tourniquet time approaching 20-30 minutes: stop, release, and reassess.
complications: Digital ischemia or amputation from a tourniquet left in place
Excessive tissue damage from prolonged exploration
aftercare: Confirm the tourniquet is off before the patient leaves the room. If a handover happens mid-procedure, the tourniquet is the first thing handed over.

Tetanus: assess the wound as clean-minor or dirty-major and the immunization history separately, and give vaccine, tetanus immune globulin, or both accordingly. See the laceration repair card, which carries the full decision.
Antibiotics for contaminated wounds, bite wounds, or immunocompromised patients per guidelines.
Wound care instructions: keep clean, dressing changes, elevation.
Return precautions: increasing pain, redness, swelling, drainage, fever, or a cold or discolored digit.
If retained FB is possible: disclose to patient, arrange follow-up, document discussion.
documentation: Foreign body removal performed from [location].
Informed consent obtained.
Pre-procedure imaging: [modality] showing [finding], and the limits of that modality for this material noted.
Local anesthesia administered: agent, concentration, and volume. Sterile technique used.
Tourniquet [used/not used]; if used, device type, application time, removal time, and total tourniquet time recorded, with post-removal perfusion documented.
Foreign body identified and removed: [description of object].
Wound irrigated with [volume] normal saline.
Post-procedure neurovascular status intact.
[Wound closed with X / wound left open for healing by secondary intention].
Tetanus status addressed with the vaccine and immune globulin decision recorded. Return precautions and follow-up discussed.
seniorPearls: If you are digging for more than 15 minutes, stop - further exploration only enlarges the wound.
Ultrasound finds much of what X-ray misses and misses things too; neither is a rule-out.
A finger tourniquet turns a bloody mess into a clean field, and costs the finger if it stays on. Write the time down.

visualAssets.title: Foreign body on ultrasound
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe. Foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures with posterior shadowing (glass, metal) or reverberation artifact. Wood shows dirty shadowing. Scan in two planes.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: X-ray misses wood, plastic, and thorns. Ultrasound is the bedside tool for radiolucent foreign bodies.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Target: C5-C7 nerve roots between anterior and middle scalene muscles.
Hemidiaphragmatic paresis is volume-dependent: at the 10-15 mL on this card, expect it often, not always. Avoid this block in severe COPD or respiratory failure regardless.
Low volume (10-15 mL); always visualize the needle tip to avoid intravascular/intraneural injection.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Shoulder dislocation (pre-reduction)
Proximal humerus fracture
Clavicle fracture (lateral third)
Complex shoulder or upper arm lacerations
contraindications: Contralateral phrenic nerve palsy or severe baseline pulmonary disease (e.g., severe COPD)
Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
Contralateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy - a second palsy obstructs the airway.
anatomy: The brachial plexus roots (C5-C7) exit between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
The 'stoplight' sign: three hypoechoic circles (C5, C6, C7 roots) stacked vertically between the scalene muscles.
The phrenic nerve runs anteriorly over the anterior scalene muscle.
The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves course through the middle scalene muscle.
The carotid artery and internal jugular vein are medial to the anterior scalene.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear transducer
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle (echogenic, short bevel, e.g., 21G or 22G, 50mm)
Local anesthetic (e.g., 10-15 mL of 0.25% or 0.5% bupivacaine or ropivacaine)
Normal saline for hydrodissection (optional but recommended)
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine or semi-recumbent with the head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked.
Place the ultrasound machine on the side of the bed opposite the provider for direct line of sight.
steps: Perform a pre-block neurovascular exam of the upper extremity.
Apply continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry, and confirm lipid emulsion availability, before injecting any volume.
Prep the lateral neck with chlorhexidine.
Place the linear probe transversely over the supraclavicular fossa to identify the subclavian artery and brachial plexus ('bunch of grapes').
Trace the brachial plexus cephalad until it forms the 'stoplight' sign between the anterior and middle scalenes.
Insert the needle in-plane from posterior to anterior (lateral to medial).
Advance the needle through the middle scalene muscle until the tip rests in the interscalene groove.
Aspirate to ensure no vascular puncture, then inject 1-2 mL to confirm spread (hydrodissection).
Inject the remaining anesthetic in 3-5 mL aliquots, aspirating between each, targeting the space around C5-C7.
Withdraw the needle and apply a sterile dressing.
ultrasound: Identify the carotid artery medially and the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) superficially.
The anterior scalene muscle lies deep to the SCM and lateral to the internal jugular vein.
The middle scalene muscle is lateral to the anterior scalene.
The nerve roots appear as hypoechoic, round structures in the fascial plane between the two scalene muscles.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid seen spreading around the C5-C7 nerve roots in the interscalene groove.
Patient reports subjective loss of sensation over the shoulder/deltoid.
Motor weakness in shoulder abduction (deltoid) and elbow flexion (biceps).
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: If the needle is difficult to see: adjust the angle of incidence, use heel-toe maneuvers, or jiggle the needle slightly.
If injection pressure is high or patient reports severe pain/paresthesia: stop immediately (possible intraneural injection). Withdraw 1-2 mm and try again.

Phrenic palsy with symptoms: sit the patient up, give oxygen, and measure rather than reassure. Escalate if the saturation falls below their baseline, the work of breathing rises, or they cannot speak in full sentences.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Phrenic nerve palsy (hemidiaphragmatic paresis) - volume-dependent, not universal
Horner syndrome (stellate ganglion block) - transient ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
Intravascular injection (vertebral or carotid artery) causing LAST
Pneumothorax (if needle advanced too far inferiorly/medially)
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Dorsal scapular or long thoracic nerve injury
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor the patient for at least 30 minutes for signs of LAST.
Place the arm in a sling to prevent traction injuries to the anesthetized limb.
Document the post-block neurovascular exam.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Indications and consent (written or verbal per policy).
Ultrasound guidance confirming spread in the interscalene groove.
No vascular puncture or intraneural injection.
Absence of immediate complications.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
seniorPearls: Tracing the plexus up from the supraclavicular fossa is often easier than starting directly at the neck.
You do not need to surround every root - the general fascial plane is usually sufficient.
Always assume you will block the phrenic nerve; do not do this block bilaterally.

The needle path crosses the middle scalene, and the dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves run through it - a reason to keep the tip in view the whole way rather than advancing to a remembered depth.

shiftMode: The 'spinal of the arm' - covers distal humerus, elbow, forearm, wrist, and hand.
Target: Brachial plexus trunks/divisions ('bunch of grapes') lateral and superficial to the subclavian artery.
High risk for pneumothorax - pleura is just deep to the artery. Always visualize the needle tip.
Keep the first rib in view as the backstop between the needle and the pleura, and do not deliberately bounce the needle off it - not a validated maneuver.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Fractures of the distal humerus, elbow, forearm, wrist, or hand
Complex lacerations or amputations of the upper extremity
Painful procedures involving the arm below the mid-humerus
contraindications: Severe baseline pulmonary disease (risk of phrenic nerve palsy or pneumothorax)
Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
anatomy: The brachial plexus at this level is tightly bundled ('bunch of grapes') lateral and superficial to the subclavian artery.
The subclavian artery rests on the first rib.
The pleura (hyperechoic line with lung sliding) lies immediately deep to the first rib and medial to the artery.
The 'corner pocket' is the space between the first rib, subclavian artery, and the brachial plexus.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear transducer
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle (echogenic, short bevel, e.g., 21G or 22G, 50mm)
Local anesthetic: 20 mL total of 0.25% or 0.5% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine, split as the steps describe.
Normal saline for hydrodissection
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine or semi-recumbent, head turned slightly away.
Arm resting comfortably at the side or across the abdomen.
steps: Perform a pre-block neurovascular exam.
Apply cardiac monitoring and ensure intralipid is available.
Prep the supraclavicular fossa.
Place the probe transversely in the supraclavicular fossa, aiming caudally to identify the subclavian artery, first rib, and pleura.
Identify the brachial plexus lateral to the artery.
Insert the needle in-plane from lateral to medial, aiming for the 'corner pocket' (the area deep to the plexus, superficial to the first rib, lateral to the artery).
Aspirate, then inject 1-2 mL of saline to confirm position.
Inject 15 mL in the corner pocket.
Withdraw the needle slightly and redirect to the superficial aspect of the plexus for the remaining 5 mL.
Remove the needle and apply a dressing.
ultrasound: Subclavian artery: large, pulsatile, anechoic circle.
First rib: hyperechoic line with posterior acoustic shadowing just deep to the artery.
Pleura: hyperechoic line medial to the rib, showing lung sliding.
Brachial plexus: hypoechoic, honeycomb-like structure ('bunch of grapes') lateral/superficial to the artery.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid spreading around the brachial plexus, especially expanding the 'corner pocket'.
Loss of sensation and motor function in the arm below the mid-humerus.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: First rib not visible: do not advance the needle. The pleura is directly underneath.
Needle lost: stop. Do not advance blindly. Use saline hydrodissection to locate the tip.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Pneumothorax (most feared complication if needle goes too deep/medial)
Phrenic nerve palsy - less common than with interscalene
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor for at least 30 minutes.
Place the arm in a sling to prevent traction injury.
Assess for shortness of breath (pneumothorax or phrenic nerve palsy).
Document post-block exam.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
Pneumothorax can declare itself hours later - tell the patient to return for new breathlessness or pleuritic pain, and hand that over.
documentation: Consent and indications.
Ultrasound guidance confirming spread in the corner pocket and around the plexus.
First rib visualized and pleura avoided.
No vascular puncture or intraneural injection.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.

seniorPearls: Aim for the first rib. If you hit the rib, you know you are safe from the pleura. Then slide up into the corner pocket.
Injecting the corner pocket first floats the plexus up and makes the rest of the block easier and safer.

shiftMode: Retroclavicular Approach to the Infraclavicular Region (RAPTIR).
Good for forearm and hand trauma - less phrenic and pleural risk than a supraclavicular block, but not zero. The needle crosses the clavicle's acoustic shadow, where the tip can't be seen.
Target: Axillary artery posterior to the pectoralis minor. The cords surround the artery.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Fractures of the forearm, wrist, or hand
Complex lacerations or amputations below the elbow
Patients in whom phrenic palsy or pneumothorax would be poorly tolerated - lower risk, not risk-free
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Coagulopathy (infraclavicular area is less compressible)
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy: deep block - ASRA applies neuraxial-equivalent timing. Use the drug-specific interval from your local antithrombotic policy.
anatomy: The brachial plexus cords (lateral, posterior, medial) surround the axillary artery deep to the pectoralis major and minor muscles.
The RAPTIR approach involves inserting the needle posterior to the clavicle, advancing caudally into the infraclavicular space.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with high-frequency linear or curvilinear transducer (depending on depth)
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle (echogenic, longer needle required, e.g., 21G 80-100mm)
Local anesthetic, standard volume: 20-30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine (30 mL = 75 mg) or 0.2% ropivacaine (30 mL = 60 mg)
Local anesthetic, higher concentration: at 0.5%, cap the volume at 20 mL (= 100 mg) and confirm the total against the weight-based maximum below before drawing up
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine, head neutral or turned slightly away.
Arm adducted and resting on the abdomen.
steps: Perform a pre-block neurovascular exam.
Apply cardiac monitoring and ensure intralipid is available.
Place the transducer in the sagittal plane over the infraclavicular fossa to identify the axillary artery and vein deep to the pectoralis muscles.
Prep the skin posterior to the clavicle.
Insert the needle posterior to the clavicle, aiming caudally, strictly in-plane with the transducer.
Advance the needle under the clavicle, visualizing the tip as it enters the ultrasound beam in the infraclavicular space.
Aim for the posterior aspect of the axillary artery (approx. 6 o'clock position).
Aspirate and inject a small test dose of saline.
Inject 20-30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine, aiming to create a U-shaped spread around the artery.
If using 0.5%, cap the volume at 20 mL and confirm the total against the weight-based maximum before injecting.
Withdraw the needle and apply a dressing.

Plan the trajectory through the retroclavicular shadow before you enter it: know the depth and angle that will bring the tip back into view, and the point at which you will abandon the approach. If the tip does not reappear where you expected, withdraw rather than explore.
ultrasound: Pectoralis major (superficial) and pectoralis minor (deep).
Axillary artery is a pulsatile anechoic circle deep to the muscles.
Axillary vein is usually medial/caudal to the artery.
The cords appear as hyperechoic dots surrounding the artery (lateral, posterior, medial).
confirmation: Anechoic fluid spreading in a U-shape or completely surrounding the axillary artery.
Loss of sensation and motor function in the arm below the elbow.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Needle trajectory unclear: withdraw and redirect. The clavicle can obstruct the view if the probe is too close.
Vein in the way: adjust the angle or use less probe pressure to avoid compressing it entirely (making it invisible).
Spread only on one side of the artery: consider a second injection site to surround it, though large volume often spreads sufficiently.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
Breathlessness, chest pain, or a falling saturation after this block: think pneumothorax and hemothorax, scan the chest, and escalate. This site does not compress.
complications: Vascular puncture (axillary artery/vein) causing hematoma or LAST
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Pneumothorax and hemothorax - part of the needle path cannot be seen
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site - the retroclavicular space does not compress
aftercare: Monitor for at least 30 minutes.
Place the arm in a sling to prevent traction injury.
Document post-block exam.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent and indications.
Ultrasound guidance confirming spread around the axillary artery.
No vascular puncture.

seniorPearls: The RAPTIR approach gives a better in-plane view of the needle approaching the artery than traditional infraclavicular approaches.
Aiming posterior to the artery (6 o'clock) usually ensures the local anesthetic spreads to all three cords.

shiftMode: Target: Radial nerve in the proximal forearm, lateral to the radial artery.
Provides anesthesia to the dorsal thumb, index, and lateral middle finger.
Block as proximal in the forearm as you can still hold the artery and nerve together.
Combine with Median/Ulnar for complete hand anesthesia.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.

Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Lacerations or fractures of the dorsal hand (radial aspect)
Procedures on the thumb or index finger (dorsal)

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
anatomy: In the proximal forearm the radial nerve runs deep to the brachioradialis, giving off several articular branches.
In the mid-forearm it is tightly associated with the lateral side of the radial artery, travelling in the same fascial plane.

equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound transducer
25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
Local anesthetic, 5-7 mL: 1% lidocaine for a short block, or 0.25% bupivacaine when the injury needs hours. Calculate the ceiling on this card before drawing up.
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel for ultrasound guidance.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you inject.
positioning: Arm supinated and extended, resting comfortably.
steps: Place the probe transversely on the volar forearm and slide it laterally to find the pulsatile radial artery.
Identify the radial nerve as a hyperechoic structure directly lateral to the artery, then slide as far proximally as you can while holding both in view.
Insert the needle in-plane.
Aspirate, then inject 5-7 mL of anesthetic around the nerve.
Confirm the anesthetic surrounding the nerve circumferentially before withdrawing.
ultrasound: Hyperechoic nerve directly lateral to the pulsatile, anechoic radial artery and in the same fascial plane.
confirmation: Anesthetic surrounding the nerve circumferentially.
Numbness in the radial nerve distribution.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.

anatomy: In the mid-forearm, the median nerve lies between the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP).
equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound transducer

Inject the rest of the 5-10 mL in increments to separate the fascial planes around the nerve.
Confirm the anesthetic spreading in the fascial plane around the nerve before withdrawing.

Mechanical coupling - needle movement visibly moving the nerve - tells you where the tip is before you commit volume to it.

Block high in the forearm, not at the wrist.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.

Lacerations or injuries to the ulnar aspect of the hand

equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound transducer

shiftMode: Target: Superficial cervical plexus as it emerges behind the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle.
Provides anesthesia to the anterior/lateral neck, clavicle, and skin over the shoulder.
Superficial block only - do not plunge deep to the SCM.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Clavicle fractures
Laceration repairs of the anterior/lateral neck or earlobe
Internal jugular vein cannulation (pain control)
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
anatomy: The plexus wraps around the posterior border of the SCM at approximately its midpoint.
The external jugular vein typically crosses the SCM near this level.
equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound transducer
25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
Local anesthetic (5-10 mL, e.g., 1% lidocaine or 0.25% bupivacaine)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel for ultrasound guidance.
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine, head turned away from the side being blocked.
steps: Place the transducer transversely over the mid-SCM.
Identify the posterior border of the SCM.
Find the external jugular vein where it crosses the SCM and keep the needle path off it.
Insert the needle in-plane from posterior to anterior.
Aspirate, then inject 5-10 mL of anesthetic in the fascial plane immediately deep to the posterior border of the SCM.
Confirm the anesthetic spreading along the posterior border of the SCM and separating the fascial layers before withdrawing.
ultrasound: SCM is the large superficial muscle. Deep to it is the levator scapulae or scalenes.
The plexus often appears as a small hyperechoic cluster at the posterior edge of the SCM.
confirmation: Anesthetic spreading along the posterior border of the SCM, separating the fascial layers.
Numbness over the neck and clavicle.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Needle tip not visible: use hydrodissection with small amounts of saline.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Phrenic nerve block (if injection is too deep/voluminous)
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
aftercare: Monitor for 30 minutes, especially for dyspnea (phrenic nerve involvement).
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through. Hand that over.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent, indications, and absence of complications.

shiftMode: Target: Fascial plane superficial OR deep to the serratus anterior muscle.
Provides analgesia to the lateral chest wall (T3-T9).
Analgesic adjunct within a rib-fracture care bundle, not a substitute for one — useful, not essential.

indications: Multiple rib fractures (lateral/anterior)
Tube thoracostomy (chest tube) placement
Chest wall abscesses or lacerations
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic

anatomy: The latissimus dorsi is the most superficial muscle on the lateral chest wall. The serratus anterior is deep to it, sitting on the ribs.

equipment: High-frequency linear transducer
Regional block needle (21G or 22G, 50-100mm)
Local anesthetic (large volume: 20-30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel for ultrasound guidance.
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine or lateral decubitus, arm abducted to expose the lateral chest (axilla).
steps: Place the transducer in the mid-axillary line at the 4th or 5th intercostal space (sagittal orientation).
Identify the latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, ribs, and pleura.
Insert the needle in-plane from cranial to caudal (or caudal to cranial).
Advance into the fascial plane either superficial to the serratus anterior (between latissimus and serratus) OR deep to the serratus anterior (between serratus and ribs).
Aspirate, then inject 20-30 mL of anesthetic.
ultrasound: Latissimus dorsi (superficial), Serratus anterior (middle), Ribs with posterior shadowing (deep), Pleura (deep to ribs with sliding).
Look for the thoracodorsal artery in the superficial plane to avoid it.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid spreading linearly along the fascial plane, unzipping the muscles.
Pain relief over the lateral chest wall.

Tip or pleura not continuously visible: stop advancing and reposition the probe until both are. If you cannot see them together, abandon the block rather than inject blind.

Regional block needle (21G or 22G, 50-100mm)

Insert the needle in-plane (usually cranial to caudal).

ultrasound: Transverse processes appear as square or rectangular hyperechoic structures with posterior shadowing (unlike the rounded ribs).

confirmation: Anechoic fluid unzipping the erector spinae muscle off the transverse processes.

shiftMode: Target: Fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
Provides analgesia to the anterior abdominal wall (parietal peritoneum and skin).
Somatic cover only. Expect deep visceral pain to remain and plan for it.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud. Calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Appendicitis pain (pre-op)
Abdominal wall abscesses or lacerations
Post-operative abdominal pain
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic

Antithrombotic therapy: not an automatic prohibition. TAP is a superficial, compressible plane block, not a deep block. Judge it on site compressibility, vascularity, and what a hematoma there would do. Follow local policy; a neuraxial hold interval does not automatically apply.
Bilateral block without a recalculated combined maximum dose (both sides share one limit)
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
anatomy: The lateral abdominal wall consists of three muscle layers: external oblique (superficial), internal oblique (middle), and transversus abdominis (deep).
The nerves supplying the abdominal wall run in the plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
equipment: High-frequency linear or curvilinear transducer
Regional block needle (21G or 22G, 80-100mm)

Local anesthetic: 20-30 mL per side of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine. Those are the strengths the labels supply, and at 30 mL a side they put a bilateral block well under the concentrations that caused trouble in the TAP pharmacokinetic studies. Do not dose up to the calculated ceiling here - read the caveat on the dose card.
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel for ultrasound guidance.
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed.
positioning: Patient supine, abdomen exposed.
steps: Place the transducer transversely on the lateral abdominal wall, midway between the costal margin and the iliac crest (mid-axillary line).
Identify the three muscle layers.
Insert the needle in-plane from anterior to posterior (or vice-versa).
Advance the needle until the tip pops through the fascia of the internal oblique into the TAP plane.
Aspirate, then inject 20-30 mL of anesthetic in 3-5 mL increments with repeat aspiration, staying under the calculated maximum dose.
ultrasound: Look for the 'three stripes' of muscle. The deepest stripe (transversus abdominis) sits right above the peritoneum/bowel.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid spreading linearly, creating a black elliptical space separating the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target territory before starting: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared with the other side.

equipment: 25G or 27G needle (short, 1 inch is fine)

steps: Identify the specific tooth causing pain.
Apply topical anesthetic to the mucobuccal fold directly above that tooth.
Retract the upper lip/cheek.
Insert the needle at the height of the mucobuccal fold, angled toward the apex (root) of the tooth.
Advance a few millimeters until the tip is near the bone (do not scrape the periosteum excessively, it hurts).
Aspirate, then inject 1-2 mL of anesthetic.

confirmation: Numbness of the specific tooth and surrounding gingiva.

anatomy: The ear is supplied by multiple nerves coming from different directions.

equipment: 25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)

steps: Cleanse the skin around the entire ear.
Insert the needle just inferior to the earlobe. Inject subcutaneously while tracking anteriorly in front of the tragus.

Insert the needle just superior to the ear. Track anteriorly to meet the first track.
From the superior puncture site, track posteriorly to meet the second track.
This creates a complete ring of anesthetic around the base of the ear.
